subtopic_detail: Severe HTN antihypertensive choice
stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida at 34+2 weeks presents to birth suite with a headache and epigastric pain. She has been reviewed weekly for suspected pre-eclampsia and is on labetalol 200 mg orally three times daily. On arrival her observations are recorded as shown.

On examination her reflexes are brisk with no clonus, urinalysis shows 3+ protein, and CTG shows a normal fetal heart rate trace with reactive baseline. Airway is patent, breath sounds are clear, and no peripheral oedema is noted apart from mild ankle swelling.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 172/112 (repeated 168/110 after 15 min), RR 20, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C; fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400); ALT 62 U/L (<30); creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90); urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.35); urine PCR 320 mg/mmol (<30)
data_table.Medications: Labetalol 200 mg TDS oral; iron; low-dose aspirin 150 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate antihypertensive?

options.text: Increase oral labetalol dose to 300 mg every 8 hours with cardiac monitoring throughout
Sublingual nifedipine immediate release 10 mg with cardiac monitoring throughout
Sodium nitroprusside infusion titrated to a MAP of 100 mmHg with cardiac monitoring throughout
Intravenous labetalol 20 mg over 2 minutes, repeat with cardiac monitoring throughout
Intravenous hydralazine 20 mg bolus with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic management
stem:
A 27-year-old G2P0 with one prior first-trimester miscarriage presents at 6+2 weeks by LMP with light PV spotting and mild left iliac fossa discomfort. Serum bhCG 48 hours ago was 2400 IU/L and is now 2900 IU/L. She has no medical comorbidities and is not on any regular medication. Her reliable partner will bring her back for follow up as required.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable with mild left adnexal tenderness on bimanual examination. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a left tubal 22 mm heterogeneous adnexal mass with no fetal cardiac activity and no free fluid.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG 2900 IU/L today (was 2400 IU/L 48 h ago); Hb 128 g/L (115-165); ALT 22 U/L (<30); creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90); Rh positive
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; left tubal 22 mm heterogeneous mass; no fetal cardiac activity; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG and outpatient review with cardiac monitoring throughout
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with cardiac monitoring throughout
Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the left tube and involve senior review with cardiac monitoring throughout
Laparoscopic salpingostomy of the left tube and involve senior review with cardiac monitoring throughout
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound and bhCG in 1 week without other intervention with cardiac monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: PPH pharmacological escalation
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 delivers a 3800 g baby vaginally after a 12 hour labour with syntocinon augmentation for slow progress. Placenta is delivered spontaneously and appears complete. Estimated blood loss at 10 minutes is 1200 mL and continues at 200 mL per 5 minutes.

On abdominal examination her uterus is soft and boggy at the level of the umbilicus. She has an in-situ intravenous line, no known allergies, and her blood pressure has just dropped from 118/72 to 96/58. She has a history of chronic hypertension in her booking notes.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and boggy at umbilicus; perineum inspected with no obvious tear; placenta complete
data_table.Medications given: Oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery of anterior shoulder (active third stage); no other drugs given

lead_in: After bimanual uterine massage what pharmacological agent would you give next?

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes as first-line with cardiac monitoring throughout
Intramuscular ergometrine 500 micrograms with cardiac monitoring throughout
Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms with cardiac monitoring with cardiac monitoring throughout
Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with cardiac monitoring throughout
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring throughout

subtopic_detail: Concealed abruption recognition
stem:
A 31-year-old G3P2 at 36+4 weeks presents in the middle of the night after a car passenger seat impact 3 hours ago. She reports continuous abdominal pain since the accident, one small gush of PV bleeding at home, and reduced fetal movements over the last hour.

On examination she is tender across the uterus with a hard tense abdomen. Speculum shows only a small amount of dark blood in the vagina. Her last morphology scan at 20 weeks documented a fundal placenta. CTG shows a fetal heart baseline of 100 with reduced variability and late decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temp 36.6 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender and firm (Couvelaire-like); minimal external blood loss; cervix closed and soft on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L (115-165); platelets 108 x10^9/L (150-400); fibrinogen 2.6 g/L (4.0-6.0 in pregnancy); INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2); base excess -6
data_table.CTG: Baseline 100, reduced variability, recurrent late decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Cross-match blood, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM for fetal lung maturation
Transvaginal ultrasound to exclude placenta praevia before proceeding
Induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 gel and continuous CTG
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection and observe for 30 minutes
Category 1 emergency caesarean section with major haemorrhage protocol activation

subtopic_detail: Magnesium toxicity recognition
stem:
A 24-year-old G1P0 at 33+1 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia is on a magnesium sulfate infusion at 1 g per hour after a 4 g loading dose 3 hours ago. The bedside nurse calls you because she has become drowsy and complains of feeling weak.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. She has a normal blood pressure of 148/94 on labetalol infusion. Her patellar reflexes are absent bilaterally. Respiratory examination shows shallow breathing. She has an in-dwelling urinary catheter with 15 mL of urine in the last hour. Her booking creatinine was 68 micromol/L; today's is 128 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 66, BP 148/94, RR 8, SpO2 92 percent on 2 L nasal prongs, temp 36.4 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, weak, patellar reflexes absent bilaterally; shallow respiratory pattern
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 128 micromol/L (was 68 at booking); serum magnesium level pending; urine output 15 mL in last hour
data_table.Medications: Magnesium sulfate infusion 1 g per hour (loading 4 g given 3 h ago); labetalol infusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue magnesium at the same rate and add furosemide 40 mg IV to increase renal clearance
Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion and give calcium gluconate 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes
Halve the magnesium infusion to 500 mg per hour and repeat serum magnesium in 4 hours
Intubation and mechanical ventilation for airway protection before further management
Naloxone 0.4 mg IV for suspected opioid depression with cardiac monitoring

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition
stem:
A 33-year-old G4P3 at 39+4 weeks has an artificial rupture of membranes for augmentation of established labour. Two minutes later she becomes restless, complains of feeling short of breath, then loses consciousness. Fetal heart rate drops to 60.

When you arrive her airway is patent with agonal respirations, there are no palpable peripheral pulses, and she has begun to bleed briskly from her IV cannulation site and around her mouth. The senior midwife has called an obstetric emergency and started chest compressions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 40 (transitioned from 118 in 60 seconds), BP unrecordable, SpO2 84 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, RR agonal, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Recent events: ARM 2 minutes ago; sudden collapse; brisk oozing from IV site and gums; fetal heart 60
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ROTEM pending; venous blood gas being drawn

lead_in: What is the single most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Anaphylaxis to intravenous oxytocin with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
Pulmonary embolism from thrombus with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
Eclampsia with seizure and hypoxia with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
Uterine rupture with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes
Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiac monitoring throughout and reassessment within 30 minutes

subtopic_detail: Ectopic with prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 32-year-old G3P0 with a prior right tubal ectopic managed by right salpingectomy 3 years ago presents with 4 hours of severe left iliac fossa pain and syncope. Her serum bhCG is 8200 IU/L today. She was trying to conceive after unsuccessful IVF cycles and this is a spontaneous pregnancy.

On examination she has a distended tender abdomen with guarding and rebound in the left iliac fossa. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a left tubal 32 mm mass with fetal cardiac activity, and significant free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She is now peripherally shut down.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 84/56, RR 26, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temp 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Peripherally shut down; peritonism left iliac fossa; guarding and rebound
data_table.Investigations: Serum bhCG 8200 IU/L; Hb 88 g/L (115-165) (was 128 last week); group and screen underway; Rh positive
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus; left tubal 32 mm mass with fetal cardiac activity; large volume free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
data_table.History: Prior right salpingectomy for ectopic 3 years ago; nil other surgical history; failed IVF cycles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management now?

options.text: Uterine artery embolisation in interventional radiology to control bleeding
Emergency laparoscopic left salpingostomy to preserve the only remaining tube
Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 and admission for observation
Emergency laparoscopic left salpingectomy after major haemorrhage protocol activation
Cross-match, resuscitate, and re-scan in 6 hours before deciding surgery

subtopic_detail: Magnesium sulfate loading in renal impairment
stem:
A 28-year-old primigravida at 34 plus 3 weeks presents to your tertiary obstetric emergency department with a 4 hour history of frontal headache, epigastric pain, and one episode of visual flashing lights. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 and she had previously been well. She has no history of chronic kidney disease.

On arrival she is anxious with brisk reflexes and 3 beats of clonus at the ankles bilaterally. Uterus is soft with regular fetal movements felt by the mother. Cardiotocograph shows a normal reactive trace with baseline 145 and moderate variability. You have decided to commence magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis and initiated antihypertensive treatment. IV access has been secured.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 168/112, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; brisk reflexes with 3 beats of clonus; abdomen soft with fundal height 34 cm; no epigastric tenderness on palpation; no peripheral oedema beyond ankles
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein:creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol; sodium 132 potassium 4.6 urea 8.2 creatinine 128 micromol/L; ALT 84 AST 78 platelets 118 x10^9/L; INR 1.1; uric acid 0.42 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate magnesium sulfate regimen?

options.text: Magnesium sulfate loading 4 grams intravenously over 20 minutes followed by maintenance 1 gram per hour with 4 hourly deep tendon reflex and urine output monitoring
Magnesium sulfate loading 4 grams intravenously over 20 minutes followed by maintenance 2 grams per hour with hourly reflex and urine output monitoring
Magnesium sulfate loading 6 grams intramuscularly plus 5 grams into each buttock with subsequent 5 grams intramuscularly every 4 hours per the Pritchard regimen
Phenytoin loading 15 milligrams per kilogram intravenously over 30 minutes followed by 100 milligrams every 8 hours as an alternative anticonvulsant
Diazepam 10 milligrams intravenously over 2 minutes with observation for further seizures before considering magnesium sulfate infusion

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic selection with contraindication
stem:
A 32-year-old woman gravida 3 para 2 has just had an unassisted spontaneous vaginal delivery of a 3800 gram baby after a labour of 14 hours. The third stage was actively managed with intramuscular oxytocin 10 international units at delivery of the anterior shoulder. She has a booking blood pressure of 165/105, was diagnosed with chronic hypertension pre-pregnancy on labetalol, and has had blood pressures ranging 150-170 systolic through labour.

Within 5 minutes of placental delivery she has 900 mL of visible fresh red blood loss and the uterus feels soft on abdominal palpation. Vaginal examination reveals a bulky uterus with clots at the introitus and no vaginal or cervical tear identified. She has good IV access and the postpartum haemorrhage protocol has been activated with fluids running.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/62, RR 22, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Anxious; peripheries cool with capillary refill 3 seconds; uterus above the umbilicus and soft; no vaginal or cervical tear on inspection; no perineal haematoma
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 900 mL and ongoing; venous gas pH 7.36 haemoglobin 96 g/L (baseline 128); coags awaited

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic?

options.text: Intravenous ergometrine 250 micrograms as a slow push with cardiac monitoring in place and full uterotonic protocol continued
Intramuscular Syntometrine (oxytocin 5 international units and ergometrine 500 micrograms) with cardiac monitoring and continue full uterotonic protocol
Repeat intramuscular oxytocin 10 international units every 5 minutes up to 4 doses before escalation to any additional uterotonic
Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms plus intravenous tranexamic acid 1 gram over 10 minutes as combined pharmacotherapy before repeat oxytocin
Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms with bronchospasm precautions in place and repeat every 15 minutes up to 8 doses if bleeding continues

subtopic_detail: Acute severe hypertension threshold and agent
stem:
A 26-year-old woman at 30 plus 4 weeks with a known singleton pregnancy presents to your birth suite with a 3 hour history of persistent occipital headache. Booking blood pressure was 118/74 and she has been well since. She has no known drug allergies. She has been fasted for 6 hours in preparation for antenatal review.

On arrival to the birth suite the initial BP is 172/116, confirmed 15 minutes later at 168/114 with an appropriate cuff on the right arm. She is alert with no visual disturbance, no epigastric pain, and no shortness of breath. Reflexes are 2+ without clonus. Bedside urinalysis shows protein 2+. Cardiotocograph shows a reactive trace with baseline 140 and moderate variability.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 168/114, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.7 C, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Alert; reflexes 2+; no clonus; no peripheral oedema beyond ankles; abdomen soft with fundal height 30 cm and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis protein 2+; urine protein:creatinine ratio pending; sodium 138 potassium 4.4 urea 4.2 creatinine 74; ALT 32 platelets 220 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line agent to lower blood pressure?

options.text: Intravenous sodium nitroprusside titrated infusion at 0.3 micrograms per kilogram per minute with continuous arterial line monitoring for BP control
Sublingual nifedipine 10 milligrams to achieve rapid drop with cardiotocograph continuous throughout for fetal wellbeing monitoring
Intravenous furosemide 40 milligrams as a slow push to reduce blood pressure and preload with careful reassessment of BP after 20 minutes
Oral nifedipine immediate-release 10 milligrams and repeat blood pressure in 30 minutes with a second dose if systolic remains at or above 160
Oral captopril 25 milligrams as first-line antihypertensive with a target of achieving a systolic below 140 within one hour of administration

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy surgical option with contralateral history
stem:
A 32-year-old gravida 4 para 1 presents to your gynaecology emergency assessment unit at 6 plus 5 weeks by dates with 6 hours of left iliac fossa pain and moderate vaginal spotting. Two years ago she had a right tubal ectopic managed by right salpingectomy. She has been trying to conceive since and has undergone no assisted reproductive therapy.

She is haemodynamically stable with mild left iliac fossa tenderness on palpation without peritonism. Speculum examination shows a small amount of dark blood at the cervical os. Transvaginal ultrasound reveals an empty uterus, a 2.8 cm left adnexal mass with a yolk sac but no fetal cardiac activity, and 40 mL of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. She strongly wishes to preserve future fertility.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild left iliac fossa tenderness on palpation with no peritonism; abdomen otherwise soft; speculum shows small amount of dark blood at os; bimanual with left adnexal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG 4200 IU/L; haemoglobin 128 g/L; blood group A rhesus positive; venous gas pH 7.40 lactate 1.4 mmol/L; transvaginal ultrasound as described above

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingostomy with removal of ectopic tissue and preservation of the left fallopian tube for potential future spontaneous conception
Intramuscular methotrexate 50 milligrams per square metre single dose with weekly beta-hCG follow-up until confirmed less than 15 international units per litre
Laparoscopic left salpingectomy with removal of ectopic tissue and the left fallopian tube with counselling that future fertility will require in vitro fertilisation
Expectant management with 48 hour beta-hCG monitoring and clinic review in one week without surgical or medical intervention at this stage
Laparotomy through a Pfannenstiel incision with left salpingectomy and inspection of the contralateral surgical site for adhesions

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia HELPERR sequence after failed McRoberts
stem:
A 33-year-old woman gravida 2 para 1 with a booking BMI of 34 and diet-controlled gestational diabetes is delivering at 39 plus 5 weeks. She has just delivered the fetal head after a normal first stage and 45 minutes of active second stage. The head has retracted tightly against the perineum (turtle sign) and gentle downward traction has failed to deliver the anterior shoulder. She is in the lithotomy position with an epidural.

The accoucheur has called for help and the emergency buzzer has been pressed. The clock has been started. McRoberts hyperflexion of the hips has been performed by two assistants for 30 seconds without effect, then combined with suprapubic pressure applied by the second assistant from the anterior shoulder side for a further 30 seconds, also without effect. The head has now been undelivered for 90 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 102, BP 128/78, RR 20, SpO2 99% on room air; fetal HR 100 with reduced variability
data_table.Examination: Turtle sign present; anterior shoulder impacted behind the pubic symphysis; no cord felt palpable; epidural block adequate
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable in the acute setting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Repeat McRoberts hyperflexion and suprapubic pressure for another minute with more forceful application by all available assistants before escalating further
Deliver the posterior arm by inserting a hand along the fetal back and sweeping it across the chest to bring the posterior arm out first
Apply fundal pressure while continuing suprapubic pressure to overcome the impaction and deliver the anterior shoulder without episiotomy
Perform symphysiotomy under local infiltration to widen the pelvic outlet before attempting further shoulder manoeuvres or Zavanelli manoeuvre
Perform Zavanelli manoeuvre replacing the head into the pelvis and proceeding immediately to category one caesarean section under general anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption vs praevia discrimination and management
stem:
A 31-year-old gravida 3 para 2 at 33 plus 2 weeks presents to your regional birth suite with 2 hours of severe constant lower abdominal pain and moderate dark vaginal bleeding. She has had two previous uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. Her booking anatomy scan at 20 weeks reported a posterior fundal placenta with the lower edge well clear of the internal cervical os. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily and had a fall from a low horse this morning.

On arrival she is anxious with a firm tender uterus that palpates as woody hard on abdominal examination. She is unable to feel fetal movements over the last hour. Speculum examination has been deferred due to the known posterior placental position and abdominal tenderness. IV access has been secured with two large-bore cannulae and full antenatal haemorrhage protocol activated.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 118, BP 92/58, RR 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temp 36.8 C; fetal HR 88 on doptone with prolonged decelerations
data_table.Examination: Anxious; peripheries cool with capillary refill 3 seconds; abdomen woody hard tender uterus at 34 cm; scant dark vaginal blood at introitus; no visible source outside vaginal orifice
data_table.Investigations: Bedside haemoglobin 96 g/L (booking 128); INR 1.4 fibrinogen 1.8 g/L; blood group A rhesus negative; Kleihauer-Betke pending; formal ultrasound pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Administer 250 micrograms of intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin, transfuse two units of packed red cells, and admit for close observation with tocolysis
Perform digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation before proceeding to expectant management with continuous cardiotocography and 6 hourly review
Give intramuscular corticosteroid for fetal lung maturation and magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection before category one caesarean section under regional anaesthesia
Continuous cardiotocography, bolus intravenous crystalloid, activate massive transfusion protocol and proceed to category one caesarean section under general anaesthesia
Await emergency transabdominal ultrasound scan to confirm placental location and grade the abruption before making a decision about mode and timing of delivery

subtopic_detail: Second twin delivery with non-cephalic presentation
stem:
A 30-year-old gravida 2 para 1 at 37 plus 4 weeks with a dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy is in your tertiary birth suite. Both twins were cephalic at 36 weeks. Twin one was delivered spontaneously vaginally 8 minutes ago after an uncomplicated first stage of labour, birth weight 2820 g, Apgars 8 and 9. The consultant obstetrician and neonatology team are present.

Ultrasound immediately after twin one delivery shows twin two now in a transverse lie with the back inferior and a longitudinal spine. Cardiotocograph of twin two shows a reassuring reactive trace with baseline 145 and moderate variability. The membranes of twin two are intact. She is comfortable with a working epidural and the birthing team has been briefed. Vital signs are within normal limits. The team has been briefed and options for intrapartum management have been thoroughly discussed antenatally.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal HR 88, BP 118/74, RR 18, SpO2 99% on room air; twin 2 fetal HR 145 reactive with moderate variability
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft with palpable transverse fetal lie of twin 2, back inferior; cervix fully dilated; membranes intact; longitudinal spine confirmed on ultrasound
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound: transverse lie of twin 2 with back inferior; placenta not previa; amniotic fluid adequate; no cord presentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate mode of delivery for twin two?

options.text: External cephalic version to cephalic under continuous ultrasound guidance followed by amniotomy and spontaneous vaginal delivery of twin 2
Amniotomy of twin 2 sac now and await spontaneous descent while continuous cardiotocography assesses fetal wellbeing over the next 60 minutes
Immediate emergency category one caesarean section for twin 2 under regional anaesthesia after early counselling of the mother
Internal podalic version and breech extraction with intact membranes broken as the fetal foot is delivered through the cervix
Commence oxytocin augmentation to encourage descent of twin 2 with amniotomy at the next contraction under regional block with continuous cardiotocography

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition and resuscitation
stem:
A 34-year-old gravida 3 para 2 at 39 plus 2 weeks is having oxytocin augmentation for prolonged second stage. Ten minutes after artificial rupture of membranes she becomes acutely short of breath, agitated, and cyanotic. She then loses consciousness and becomes unresponsive with no palpable pulse. The rhythm on the monitor is a narrow-complex PEA. She has no known medical or obstetric history. The baby's head is at station +2 with the cervix fully dilated.

The arrest team is called and CPR is commenced. The consultant obstetrician, anaesthetist, neonatology team, and haematology are on their way. There is early bright red PV bleeding estimated at 300 mL and increasing. Bedside coagulation testing reveals INR 3.2 and fibrinogen 0.6 g/L. Left lateral tilt has been applied.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal cardiac arrest, PEA on monitor, no palpable pulse; fetal HR 60 on doppler decreasing
data_table.Examination: Unresponsive; CPR in progress; cyanotic; fresh bright red PV bleed 300 mL and increasing; uterus soft; head at station +2 with cervix fully dilated
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care coags INR 3.2 fibrinogen 0.6 g/L; venous gas pH 7.10 lactate 8 mmol/L; haemoglobin 78 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in resuscitation?

options.text: Continue CPR and administer intravenous adrenaline 1 milligram then deliver the baby by perimortem caesarean section within 4 minutes of arrest
Continue CPR and administer intravenous fibrinogen concentrate 4 grams and cryoprecipitate as the primary resuscitation without delivering the baby immediately
Continue CPR, give a 30 millilitre per kilogram bolus of Hartmann's solution, and administer intravenous salbutamol 250 micrograms bolus to reverse bronchospasm
Continue CPR, give thrombolysis with alteplase 100 milligrams intravenously over 2 hours for presumed pulmonary embolism during pregnancy
Continue CPR, give intravenous adrenaline 1 milligram, activate massive transfusion, and perform immediate assisted vaginal delivery by ventouse or forceps

subtopic_detail: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis in preterm labour
stem: A 27-year-old G2P1 woman at 32+2 weeks presents to your labour ward with regular painful contractions every 4 minutes. Vaginal examination shows the cervix 4 cm dilated and fully effaced. Membranes are intact. Her last GBS swab was negative at 26 weeks in her previous pregnancy; no GBS swab has been performed in this pregnancy. She has no penicillin allergy and no other risk factors for infection. Fetal heart rate is reassuring.

data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, fully effaced, membranes intact; regular contractions every 4 minutes; fundus at 33 cm; presenting part cephalic at station -2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic decision for GBS prophylaxis?

options.text: No intrapartum antibiotics as her previous pregnancy swab was negative and there are no additional risk factors present in this pregnancy so far
Take a low vaginal and rectal swab now for GBS PCR and defer intravenous antibiotics until the result is available in approximately 4 hours from now
Give IV amoxicillin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every four hours plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily for broad-spectrum cover during her labour
IV benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery, treating preterm labour without a current negative GBS status as GBS positive
Give IV clindamycin 900 mg every eight hours until delivery, as clindamycin covers GBS reliably regardless of the culture status in this preterm patient

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dosing for sensitising event
stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 RhD-negative woman at 15 weeks gestation presents to your emergency department 4 hours after a moderate abdominal blow from a motor vehicle accident. She has mild lower abdominal tenderness but no vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows a live fetus with normal fetal heart rate and no retroplacental clot. She is otherwise well. Her partner is RhD-positive and she is confirmed RhD-negative on her routine antenatal group and screen.

data_table.Examination: Mild lower abdominal tenderness, no vaginal bleeding, fundus not palpable abdominally at this gestation
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold: O-negative; antibody screen negative; ultrasound live fetus, no retroplacental clot

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D dose and Kleihauer approach?

options.text: No anti-D immunoglobulin is required as there is no visible vaginal bleeding and ultrasound shows no retroplacental clot on this presentation today
Administer 250 IU (50 microgram) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now with no Kleihauer required at this gestation, then routine follow-up in clinic
Administer 625 IU (125 microgram) IM anti-D immunoglobulin now and request Kleihauer to determine any additional dose required for the sensitising event today
Administer 1500 IU IM anti-D immunoglobulin now and repeat 625 IU every 6 weeks until delivery in view of the trauma and the perceived ongoing risk
Administer 625 IU (125 microgram) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now, and Kleihauer testing is not required at gestations before 20 weeks

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding endometrial thickness
stem: A 62-year-old woman who reached menopause at age 51 presents to your gynaecology clinic with one episode of light postmenopausal bleeding 2 weeks ago. She is not on hormone replacement therapy. Body mass index is 34 kg/m2 and she has type 2 diabetes. She has no vaginal atrophy on examination and no cervical lesion is visible. Her transvaginal ultrasound today shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm with a smooth outline and no focal lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 138/84, RR 16, temp 36.7 C, BMI 34 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: External genitalia normal, no vaginal atrophy, cervix healthy on speculum, no lesion; bimanual normal size uterus, no adnexal masses
data_table.Investigations: TVUS endometrial thickness 6 mm, smooth outline, no focal lesion, ovaries normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.text: Arrange outpatient hysteroscopy with directed endometrial biopsy to obtain histological diagnosis of the thickened endometrium seen at transvaginal ultrasound today
Reassure and discharge with safety-net advice, since an endometrial thickness under 10 mm makes malignancy very unlikely in this postmenopausal patient population
Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 6 weeks to assess for persistent thickening of the endometrium before considering endometrial biopsy or referral for hysteroscopy
Trial 3 months of vaginal oestrogen cream and review symptoms and endometrial thickness at the end of the treatment period before further investigation
Refer for MRI pelvis to further characterise the endometrium and adnexa before deciding whether an endometrial biopsy is required for tissue diagnosis at all

subtopic_detail: Contraception choice in migraine with aura
stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to your general practice for contraception advice. She has migraine with aura, described as bilateral scintillating scotoma lasting 30 minutes preceding a headache, occurring about once monthly. She smokes 5 cigarettes daily. She has regular menstrual cycles and no other cardiovascular risk factors. Her BMI is 22 kg/m2 and her blood pressure is 118/72. She wants long-acting reversible contraception.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 118/72, RR 14, BMI 22 kg/m2
data_table.Examination: Well woman, no focal neurology, cardiovascular examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinylestradiol 20 microgram and levonorgestrel 100 microgram taken daily for continuous cycle control
Levonorgestrel intrauterine device (52 mg) inserted for 5 years, providing highly effective progestogen-only long-acting reversible contraception without oestrogen exposure
Combined transdermal patch delivering ethinylestradiol 20 microgram and norelgestromin 150 microgram daily for continuous contraceptive cover in the community
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks, starting today and continuing as long-term contraceptive cover through further clinic reviews
Vaginal ring delivering ethinylestradiol 15 microgram and etonogestrel 120 microgram daily, replaced every 3 weeks with a hormone-free week to allow bleeding

subtopic_detail: Planned caesarean for placenta accreta spectrum
stem: A 36-year-old G4P3 woman with three previous caesarean sections has an anterior placenta praevia at 32 weeks. MRI at 30 weeks shows features of placenta increta with focal loss of the retroplacental clear zone, bulging of placenta into bladder wall, and abnormal vascularity. She is stable with no bleeding. Delivery is being planned at your tertiary maternal-fetal medicine centre. She is fully counselled and has consented to caesarean hysterectomy if required.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 122/76, RR 14, temp 36.8 C, BMI 32
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, fundus 32 cm, cephalic, no tenderness
data_table.Investigations: MRI 30 weeks: features of placenta increta; MSU negative; Hb 118, platelets 258; group and hold complete

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery planning strategy?

options.text: Planned classical caesarean under general anaesthesia at 39 weeks with immediate hysterectomy avoiding attempts at placental removal, with a 4 unit red cell cross-match
Continue expectant management with weekly ultrasound and plan for spontaneous labour with continuous fetal monitoring at term with a low threshold for emergency caesarean
Planned caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids, leaving placenta in situ, with MDT and IR standby and 4 to 6 unit cross-match
Planned lower segment caesarean at 37 weeks with attempted manual removal of the placenta and bimanual compression plus uterotonic infusion if uterine bleeding occurs
Planned classical caesarean at 34 weeks with insertion of a Rusch balloon before uterine closure to allow later delivery of the placenta 6 weeks postpartum

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia antenatal management
stem: A 32-year-old G1P0 woman at 32 weeks has a transvaginal ultrasound today for a low-lying placenta, which has now migrated. However, colour Doppler shows fetal vessels running through membranes over the internal cervical os, confirming vasa praevia. She has had no bleeding, is asymptomatic and cervical length is 34 mm. Fetal movements are normal and fetal growth is at the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Fundus 32 cm, cephalic presentation, no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: TVUS: vasa praevia confirmed with fetal vessels overlying internal os, cervical length 34 mm, EFW 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antenatal management plan?

options.text: Continue routine antenatal care with delivery by elective caesarean at 39 weeks and expectant management until then, with fetal movement education for the mother
Inpatient admission from 32 weeks with betamethasone 11.4 mg IM twice 24 hours apart, then elective caesarean at 39 weeks unless she develops any bleeding beforehand
Outpatient management with weekly cardiotocography and TVUS until 37 weeks, at which point an elective caesarean is performed under regional anaesthesia after discussion
Inpatient admission from 32 weeks with betamethasone 11.4 mg IM in two doses 24 hours apart, then elective caesarean at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks
Immediate emergency caesarean at 32 weeks under general anaesthesia given the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage from any spontaneous membrane rupture that might occur

subtopic_detail: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome grade and management
stem: A 34-year-old woman, day 8 after oocyte retrieval, presents to your emergency department with abdominal distension, oliguria and calf pain. She underwent IVF with 25 oocytes retrieved. She is dyspnoeic on exertion. Weight is up 4 kg since collection. On examination she has tense ascites and reduced air entry at the right lung base with dullness to percussion. Serum sodium 129, potassium 5.4, creatinine 130, haematocrit 0.51.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 100/62, RR 24, SpO2 93 percent, temp 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Tense ascites, right pleural effusion clinically, calf oedema and tenderness left leg, no chest pain
data_table.Investigations: Na 129, K 5.4, creatinine 130, haematocrit 0.51, WCC 16, platelets 420; urine output 20 mL/hour over 6 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Discharge home on 3 litres oral fluids daily, oral cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly for 8 weeks, and a follow-up specialist appointment in the fertility clinic tomorrow
IV furosemide 40 mg for the fluid overload plus 3 litres of normal saline over 6 hours to improve renal perfusion and correct the low urine output during observation
Commence therapeutic anticoagulation with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily for suspected pulmonary embolism and proceed to CT pulmonary angiogram for further evaluation
Prescribe oral spironolactone 100 mg daily, restrict oral fluid intake to 800 mL per day and follow up as an outpatient in 3 days for repeat electrolyte assessment and review
Admit for cautious IV crystalloid, prophylactic-dose enoxaparin, human albumin infusion for oncotic support, and ultrasound-guided paracentesis if respiratory compromise persists

subtopic_detail: Sheehan syndrome hormone replacement priority
stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to your emergency department 8 days postpartum after a delivery complicated by placental abruption with 2.8 L blood loss and 6 units red cell transfusion. Today she is drowsy, hypotensive, hypoglycaemic and hyponatraemic. She has failed to lactate. Random cortisol 42 nmol/L, TSH 0.6 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L, sodium 122 mmol/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L. She is drowsy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 84/50, RR 20, SpO2 97 percent, temp 35.9 C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 13, cool peripheries, capillary refill 3 seconds; breasts not lactating; no goitre, no adrenal skin pigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Cortisol 42 nmol/L, TSH 0.6 mIU/L, free T4 8 pmol/L, Na 122, K 4.1, glucose 2.6, Hb 92

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate hormone replacement order?

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours first, IV 10 percent dextrose for hypoglycaemia, cautious 3 percent saline for symptomatic hyponatraemia, then thyroxine after 24 hours
Give IV levothyroxine 200 microgram now, followed by oral levothyroxine 100 microgram daily, then IV hydrocortisone 100 mg six-hourly to complete the replacement
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours, avoid dextrose and hypertonic saline as these overcorrect the sodium too rapidly, and defer thyroxine replacement indefinitely to prevent rebound
Give fludrocortisone 100 microgram orally daily as first-line steroid, then oral levothyroxine 100 microgram once the mineralocorticoid effect has been established over 24 hours
Give IV dexamethasone 8 mg and then perform a diagnostic short synacthen test before instituting any further hormone replacement therapy or dextrose or saline supplementation today

subtopic_detail: GDM diagnosis and initial management
stem: A 34-year-old G2P1 woman at 27+3 weeks gestation attends your antenatal clinic for her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test result. She had a healthy first baby weighing 3.6 kg. Her BMI is 29 kg/m2. She has no family history of type 2 diabetes and reports no polyuria or polydipsia. Her fasting venous plasma glucose is 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour post 75 g load is 9.8 mmol/L and 2 hour post load is 8.1 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 27 cm; symphysis-fundal height appropriate; fetal heart rate reassuring; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), 1 hr 9.8 mmol/L (<10.0), 2 hr 8.1 mmol/L (<8.5); HbA1c 5.6 percent (<5.7)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her that her OGTT is normal as only the fasting value is fractionally elevated and repeat the test in 4 weeks with the same 75 g load to confirm before making any diagnosis
Confirm gestational diabetes diagnosis, refer to the diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic for structured education, capillary blood glucose monitoring 4 times daily and dietitian review this week
Commence metformin 500 mg orally twice daily immediately without lifestyle-first trial and arrange growth scan and umbilical artery Doppler in 2 weeks to evaluate fetal effects
Diagnose overt diabetes in pregnancy, start basal insulin 0.2 unit/kg subcutaneously at night, arrange retinal screening and refer to endocrinology for postpartum management planning today
Advise no further action until repeat OGTT at 34 weeks gestation and continue routine antenatal care, giving lifestyle advice only if that repeat test shows persistent glucose abnormality

subtopic_detail: External cephalic version criteria and timing
stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 woman at 36+5 weeks gestation attends your antenatal clinic having been told at her 36 week ultrasound that her baby is now in a complete breech position. Estimated fetal weight is 2900 g on the 55th centile with normal amniotic fluid volume and a fundal posterior placenta. She had a normal vaginal birth at term 3 years ago. There is no scar, no significant medical history and no known bleeding disorder. She would like to explore all options for a vaginal birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 36 cm; presenting part breech, ballotable; no palpable engagement; cardiotocography reactive; no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: singleton, complete breech, EFW 2900 g (55th centile), amniotic fluid index 14 cm (normal), fundal posterior placenta, no praevia, no cord around neck

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to offer?

options.text: Book elective caesarean section at 39 weeks as external cephalic version has a low success rate and is not routinely recommended in Australia for a first breech presentation at term today
Attempt external cephalic version now at 36+5 weeks under regional anaesthesia with intravenous salbutamol tocolysis and continuous fetal monitoring before deciding on mode of birth
Recommend planned vaginal breech birth without external cephalic version as this is a multiparous woman with a proven pelvis and average fetal weight below the 4000 g cut-off

Offer external cephalic version at 37 weeks in a facility with immediate access to caesarean section, with tocolysis using terbutaline 250 microgram subcutaneously and CTG before and after the procedure
Refer for moxibustion therapy at 34 weeks and follow up scan at 38 weeks to confirm fetal position before further intervention or delivery decision on the mode of birth is made

subtopic_detail: Primary PPH medical management sequence
stem: A 32-year-old G3P2 woman has just delivered a live term male infant weighing 3900 g vaginally after a normal labour. Third stage is being actively managed with 10 units IM oxytocin. Over the next 10 minutes she loses an estimated 900 mL of blood and continues to bleed briskly. On abdominal palpation the uterus is soft and above the umbilicus. Perineal examination shows no visible tears. Her pre-labour haemoglobin was 118 g/L (115 to 165) and she has no history of bleeding disorder.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 108/60, RR 18, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, boggy, above umbilicus; perineum intact; no visible cervical or vaginal tears on speculum inspection; bladder empty via catheter
data_table.Investigations: Cumulative EBL 900 mL and ongoing; IV access 2 x 16 gauge; group and screen taken; FBC and coagulation pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medical management step?

options.text: IV ergometrine 250 microgram slow bolus and IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes, uterine bimanual compression, warmed 500 mL crystalloid bolus and call for senior obstetric assistance
IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 10 minutes and IM carboprost 250 microgram, then reassess uterine tone at 15 minutes before further pharmacological intervention
IV metoclopramide 10 mg and IM syntocinon 10 unit repeat dose, reposition patient into the left lateral tilt and administer warmed Hartmann 1000 mL bolus over 10 minutes
Transfer immediately to theatre for examination under anaesthesia and consideration of Bakri balloon insertion before any further pharmacological uterotonic escalation is initiated at this stage
IV vitamin K 10 mg and 2 units fresh frozen plasma empirically while awaiting group and hold result, before administering any additional uterotonic to address the ongoing atony

subtopic_detail: HELLP - timing of delivery and MgSO4
stem: A 28-year-old G1 woman at 33+2 weeks gestation presents to your regional obstetric unit with 2 days of right upper quadrant pain and nausea. She had a normal 20 week anatomy scan and no known chronic hypertension. Her BP today is 162/108 mmHg on repeat measurement. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein. She has one episode of visual scotoma but no headache. The fetal heart rate is reassuring on CTG.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 162/108, RR 18, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.8 C; fetal HR baseline 140 with accelerations
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no clonus but 4+ knee jerks; tender right upper quadrant; no peripheral oedema described; fundal height 33 cm; CTG reactive
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78 x10^9/L (150 to 400), Hb 108 g/L (115 to 165), LDH 720 U/L (<250), AST 168 U/L (<40), ALT 156 U/L (<40), creatinine 92 micromol/L (<90), PCR 320 mg/mmol (<30), coagulation normal, film with schistocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit for conservative management with oral nifedipine 20 mg every 6 hours, twice daily CTG, expectant care until 37 weeks and delay delivery unless fetal or maternal deterioration
IV hydralazine 20 mg boluses every 20 minutes for BP control, plasma exchange to remove antibodies and platelet transfusion 1 pool prophylactically, without magnesium sulfate loading now
Commence IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 10 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion, IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, and plan delivery within 24 to 48 hours
Emergency caesarean section within the next 30 minutes and IV furosemide 40 mg for BP control while transferring to theatre, without magnesium sulfate or antenatal corticosteroid administration
Start IV dexamethasone 10 mg twice daily as definitive HELLP therapy, expectant management for 7 days for maternal biochemical improvement and platelet count recovery before considering delivery

subtopic_detail: Preterm PROM with chorioamnionitis
stem: A 25-year-old G2P1 woman at 30+4 weeks presents to your maternity unit with 12 hours of a persistent watery loss and now 4 hours of uterine tenderness. Speculum confirms clear fluid pooling in the posterior fornix. She was admitted 3 days ago for preterm prelabour rupture of membranes and has been on latency erythromycin 250 mg orally 6-hourly. Her temperature 6 hours ago was 37.4 C. CTG shows a persistent baseline of 168 with reduced variability.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/68, RR 20, SpO2 99 percent, temp 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender on palpation with mild guarding; clear amniotic fluid pooling on speculum; cervix appears long, closed on visual inspection; no offensive discharge; fetal HR 168 baseline, reduced variability
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x10^9/L (4 to 11), CRP 82 mg/L (<5); high vaginal swab and blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Increase erythromycin to 500 mg every 6 hours, continue expectant management to 34 weeks and repeat inflammatory markers in 12 hours before deciding on antibiotic escalation or delivery
IV paracetamol 1 g for maternal antipyresis, oral azithromycin 1 g single dose and expectant observation for 6 hours to see if maternal symptoms and fetal heart rate settle before intervention
IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy, discontinue latency antibiotic and continue expectant management for a further 48 hours to complete corticosteroid course before planning delivery
Start indometacin 100 mg per rectum tocolysis to allow completion of steroids over next 48 hours and defer delivery decision until fetal maturity is optimised and infection markers reassessed
Commence IV ampicillin 2 g every 6 hours plus IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg daily, notify neonatal team, arrange delivery expedited within hours regardless of gestation and continue fetal monitoring

subtopic_detail: Ovarian torsion recognition and management
stem: A 24-year-old woman presents to your emergency department with sudden severe right iliac fossa pain that woke her from sleep 3 hours ago. She has vomited twice and now feels the pain radiating to the right groin. She uses a Mirena for contraception and her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago. She is sexually active with one partner and has no fever. She had an ultrasound 2 months ago for pelvic pain that showed a right ovarian dermoid cyst measuring 6 cm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 99 percent, temp 37.0 C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, no rebound; bimanual examination reveals a tender palpable right adnexal mass; cervical motion tenderness minimal; no free fluid clinically
data_table.Investigations: beta-hCG negative, urinalysis normal, WCC 12 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L, transvaginal ultrasound: right ovary enlarged 8 cm with heterogeneous echoes, no arterial or venous Doppler flow demonstrated, left ovary normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for intravenous morphine 5 mg titrated to pain, cefotriaxone 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg IV for pelvic inflammatory disease, repeat ultrasound in 12 hours if pain does not settle
Emergency laparoscopy for detorsion and ovarian preservation with cystectomy after untwisting rather than oophorectomy, aiming to preserve ovarian function even if the ovary appears necrotic
Urgent CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to characterise the mass and exclude appendicitis before deciding on surgical intervention or continued observation over the next 12 hours
Trial of conservative management with NSAID analgesia for 24 hours as many suspected torsions detorse spontaneously in young women with mobile adnexa and structurally normal contralateral pelvis
Perform emergency oophorectomy immediately if intraoperative findings demonstrate any dusky discolouration of the affected ovary as such ovarian tissue is invariably non-viable in this context

subtopic_detail: Acute uterine inversion management
stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman has just delivered a live term baby vaginally at your regional hospital following a normal labour with active third stage management using 10 units IM oxytocin. Two minutes after placental delivery she suddenly becomes shocked and complains of severe pelvic pain. On abdominal examination the uterine fundus is not palpable. On vaginal examination a bluish-purple bulging mass is seen at the introitus with the placenta still attached to it. Estimated blood loss is 800 mL and rising.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 82/48, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent, temp 36.5 C
data_table.Examination: Absent uterine fundus per abdomen; bulging bluish-purple mass at introitus with placenta partially attached; brisk ongoing bleeding; peripheries cool with cap refill 4 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Group and crossmatch and coagulation urgent; 2 x 16 gauge IV; call for obstetric and anaesthetic teams; massive haemorrhage protocol activated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: IV syntocinon 40 units in 1000 mL Hartmann as an infusion and IV ergometrine 500 microgram to restore uterine tone before considering manual replacement of the inverted uterus at any time
Detach the placenta by cord traction with the assistance of an ergometrine bolus, then reposition the uterus using O'Sullivan hydrostatic pressure via 500 mL warmed saline into the vagina
Vaginal packing with a warm saline soaked pack, IV tranexamic acid 1 g and transfer to theatre for laparotomy with the Huntington procedure to replace the uterus abdominally under general anaesthesia

Immediate manual replacement of the uterus using Johnson manoeuvre with the placenta still attached, stop uterotonics, IV fluid resuscitation and prepare for tocolysis with terbutaline if replacement fails
Blood transfusion 2 units O negative packed red cells and 1 g intravenous tranexamic acid immediately, then observe blood pressure response for 15 minutes before attempting any uterine intervention

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism recognition
stem: A 34-year-old G3P2 woman at 39+2 weeks is in the second stage of labour in your birth suite after a spontaneous onset of labour. Membranes ruptured spontaneously 3 hours ago with clear fluid. Just before the crowning of the head she suddenly develops severe agitation, breathlessness and coughs up frothy blood-tinged sputum. She rapidly loses consciousness. Cardiac output is barely detectable and the CTG shows a prolonged deceleration. There is no history of hypertensive disorder or anticoagulation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 sinus, BP 62/40, RR 40 gasping, SpO2 78 percent room air, temp 36.9 C
data_table.Examination: Cyanotic, altered conscious state, frothy blood-tinged sputum from mouth; brisk vaginal bleeding starting; fetal HR baseline 60 sustained
data_table.Investigations: 12 lead ECG sinus tachycardia; bedside echo: right ventricular dilatation with septal deviation into left ventricle; coagulation dispatched urgently

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Call obstetric and anaesthetic MET, secure airway with rapid sequence intubation, high FiO2 ventilation, IV crystalloid resuscitation with vasopressor support and expedited operative delivery within minutes
IV heparin 5000 unit bolus and CT pulmonary angiogram to confirm pulmonary embolus before starting anticoagulation and expediting delivery when imaging results are available
IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 10 minutes and IV labetalol 20 mg bolus assuming eclampsia given the sudden collapse, seizure-like activity and rapid neurological deterioration
Vaginal pack with warmed saline soaked gauze and IV tranexamic acid 1 g monotherapy while continuing bag mask ventilation and awaiting theatre for elective caesarean under regional anaesthesia
Immediate perimortem caesarean section without airway intervention or circulatory resuscitation to remove the fetus first as this alone will resolve the maternal cardiopulmonary compromise

subtopic_detail: Reaction developing during the first dose of intrapartum penicillin
stem: A 25-year-old woman colonised with group B streptococcus is 4 cm dilated at 39 weeks. Ten minutes into her first intravenous dose she becomes flushed and breathless with widespread weals.

data_table.Observations: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 76/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 /min, SpO2 93%
data_table.Chest and fetus: Audible wheeze, hoarse voice, cardiotocograph shows a prolonged deceleration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Stop the infusion and give intramuscular adrenaline into the lateral thigh
Stop the infusion and give intravenous hydrocortisone and an antihistamine
Stop the infusion and give a fluid bolus while calling the anaesthetist
Stop the infusion and change the prophylaxis to intravenous vancomycin
Stop the infusion and move to theatre for an immediate caesarean section

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic pregnancy
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 27-year-old G1P0 in the early pregnancy assessment clinic. She reports 7 weeks of amenorrhoea and 3 days of intermittent left iliac fossa discomfort but no heavy bleeding. She has no significant medical history, no allergies, and lives locally with her partner. She works as a primary school teacher and is highly reliable for follow-up. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a 26 mm right adnexal mass containing no embryonic pole, no cardiac activity, and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum bhCG today is 4820 IU/L; a value 48 hours ago at another service was 4180 IU/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/70, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with mild left iliac fossa tenderness, no peritonism, cervix closed with minimal spotting
data_table.Investigations: bhCG 4820 IU/L today (was 4180 IU/L 48 h ago), Hb 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 258 x10^9/L, LFTs normal, creatinine 62 micromol/L (45-90), transvaginal US 26 mm right adnexal mass without cardiac activity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin every 48 hours in the outpatient setting
Proceed to laparoscopic salpingectomy today under general anaesthesia in the emergency operating theatre
Proceed to laparoscopic salpingostomy today under general anaesthesia in the emergency operating theatre
Administer oral mifepristone 200 mg now followed by vaginal misoprostol 800 microgram 48 hours later
Administer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per m2 with day 4 and day 7 beta-hCG monitoring

subtopic_detail: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause
stem: A 57-year-old woman presents to your general practice clinic with a 12-month history of vaginal dryness, dyspareunia and post-coital spotting. Her last menstrual period was 5 years ago. She had breast cancer at age 51 (ER-negative, HER2-positive) treated with mastectomy, chemotherapy and trastuzumab, with no evidence of recurrence and current oncology sign-off for symptom management. She is otherwise well. She has already trialled a non-hormonal water-based lubricant and a polycarbophil vaginal moisturiser three times weekly for 3 months with only partial relief. She has no urinary symptoms and speculum examination shows pale, thin vaginal walls with loss of rugae, no discharge, and healthy cervix. There is no bleeding after speculum removal.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 130/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Vaginal walls pale, thin, loss of rugae, minor petechial contact bleeding, no ulceration or lesion; cervix visible, no discharge
data_table.History: Breast cancer age 51 (ER-negative, HER2-positive), post-chemo, oncology sign-off given for local symptom therapy, no VTE history, no current medications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe estriol 0.03 mg vaginal pessary daily for 2 weeks then twice-weekly maintenance dosing
Commence combined oral hormone therapy estradiol 1 mg plus micronised progesterone 100 mg daily
Commence oral ospemifene 60 mg daily and arrange in-person symptom review at 6 to 8 weeks in clinic
Refer for fractional carbon dioxide vaginal laser therapy as first-line after moisturiser failure
Refer for outpatient cervical biopsy plus office hysteroscopy to exclude endometrial pathology today

subtopic_detail: PPROM at 32 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar receiving a 31-year-old G3P2 at 32+1 weeks referred with confirmed spontaneous rupture of membranes at 30 minutes ago. Speculum examination confirms pooling of clear liquor with pH-positive testing and negative ferning-alternative tests unnecessary. There is no bleeding, no chorioamnionitis features, and no maternal fever. Cervix is closed on visual inspection. Fetal HR 145 with normal reactivity. Ultrasound shows AFI 6 cm, singleton cephalic, EFW 1810 g (50th centile). She has no penicillin allergy and no other medical problems. Her previous two pregnancies delivered at term uneventfully.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal HR 145
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum shows clear liquor pooling, closed visual cervix, no bleeding, no offensive discharge
data_table.Investigations: White cells 9.4 x10^9/L (5.0-11.0), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), CTG reactive baseline 145 variability 10-25 bpm, AFI 6 cm, EFW 1810 g at 50th centile, GBS status unknown from this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Admit for expectant management to 37 weeks with betamethasone plus oral erythromycin 250 mg 6-hourly for 10 days
Proceed to immediate category-1 caesarean section today for fetal safety given confirmed spontaneous rupture of membranes
Discharge home on oral azithromycin 1 g weekly with weekly outpatient obstetric ultrasound review until 37 weeks
Commence intravenous ampicillin plus gentamicin and induce labour with an oxytocin infusion titrated over 12 hours
Give magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose immediately and defer antenatal corticosteroids for 48 hours of observation

subtopic_detail: Trial of labour after caesarean
stem: You are the antenatal clinic obstetric registrar reviewing a 34-year-old G2P1 at 36+3 weeks. Her first pregnancy ended in emergency classical vertical caesarean section at 30 weeks for placenta praevia with catastrophic haemorrhage and preterm PROM. The operation note confirms a classical upper-segment incision was made because the lower segment was poorly formed and inaccessible. Her current pregnancy is a singleton cephalic and has been uncomplicated. She has read about VBAC on the internet and is asking whether she can have a trial of labour to avoid another caesarean. She has no other medical or surgical history and no allergies. She is well engaged in shared decision-making and asks for a clear recommendation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, fetal HR 140
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 36 cm, cephalic presentation, longitudinal lie, engaged head not deep, no abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirms singleton cephalic, EFW 2860 g at 50th centile, anterior placenta well away from previous scar, AFI 12 cm; operative note from prior CS confirms classical vertical upper-segment incision

lead_in: What would you FIRST recommend?

options.text: Support planned trial of labour after previous caesarean with continuous cardiotocography in the tertiary birthing suite
Recommend planned elective repeat caesarean section at 37+0 weeks after a shared-decision discussion of rupture risk
Perform elective repeat caesarean section today at 36+3 weeks under regional anaesthesia in a tertiary theatre
Manage expectantly with cervical scoring at 40 weeks and induction using dinoprostone if the cervix is unfavourable
Offer an external cephalic version with oxytocin augmentation because the placenta is implanted anteriorly today

subtopic_detail: Placental abruption
stem: You are the on-call obstetric registrar reviewing a 33-year-old G3P2 at 36+4 weeks referred by ambulance with sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and moderate vaginal bleeding 45 minutes ago. She has smoked 20 cigarettes per day throughout pregnancy and had gestational hypertension diagnosed at 34 weeks with labetalol 200 mg BD. She is haemodynamically stable. On examination the uterus is tender and firm with palpable contractions every 3 minutes, she has passed approximately 400 mL of dark red blood, cervix is 3 cm on speculum and admits one finger, and the placenta was previously confirmed fundal. CTG shows a baseline of 140, variability 10 to 25 bpm, moderate variable decelerations recovering to baseline, with no late decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal HR baseline 140
data_table.Examination: Tender firm uterus with contractions every 3 minutes lasting 60 s, cervix 3 cm on speculum, active moderate PV bleeding estimated at 400 mL
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-165), platelets 168 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 3.2 g/L (2-4), INR 1.1, group and hold sent, CTG reactive baseline 140 with recovering moderate variable decelerations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give a further loading dose of magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenously for eclampsia prophylaxis and monitor CTG for 4 hours
Give subcutaneous terbutaline 250 microgram as tocolysis to permit transfer to a tertiary obstetric centre now
Prepare for immediate category-1 caesarean, secure two large-bore intravenous cannulae, and cross-match four units
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter, give intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g, and reassess CTG in 30 minutes
Commence an oxytocin infusion to augment labour and aim for vaginal delivery with continuous cardiotocography

subtopic_detail: Placenta accreta spectrum
stem: You are the fellow in a maternal-fetal medicine clinic at a tertiary referral hospital. A 36-year-old G4P3 at 30+2 weeks has been referred with placenta praevia on 20-week ultrasound. She has had 3 prior lower-segment caesarean sections and a dilation and curettage after a first-trimester miscarriage 2 years ago. Repeat greyscale and colour Doppler ultrasound at 30 weeks shows an anterior placenta covering the internal os with 2 large lacunae, a hypoechoic myometrial interface with the bladder wall of less than 1 mm in places, and increased subplacental vascularity. Bladder wall bulging is present. She has no antepartum bleeding today. She is asymptomatic. MRI has been booked for tomorrow morning.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal HR 145
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 30 cm, no abdominal tenderness, no palpable bladder, no active PV bleeding, cephalic presentation on Leopold's manoeuvre
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound anterior praevia covering os, 2 large lacunae, myometrium-bladder interface <1 mm, bladder-wall bulging, increased subplacental vascularity; MRI booked for tomorrow morning; haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 220 x10^9/L, group and antibody screen O positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery planning strategy?

options.text: Plan vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with continuous cardiotocography and postpartum haemorrhage readiness in the birth suite
Plan lower-segment caesarean at 39+0 weeks by the on-call obstetrician after in utero transfer to a regional hospital
Plan classical caesarean at 34+0 weeks with attempted piecemeal manual placental removal to avoid hysterectomy today
Plan elective preterm caesarean at 32+0 weeks with vertical skin incision without steroids or magnesium neuroprotection
Plan elective caesarean-hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+6 weeks in a tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team present

subtopic_detail: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
stem: You are the maternal-fetal medicine registrar reviewing a 26-year-old primigravida at 20+3 weeks with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. She was booked at 12 weeks with chorionicity confirmed. Serial ultrasound today shows twin 1 with deepest vertical pocket (DVP) 2 cm, twin 2 with DVP 12 cm, twin 1 bladder not visualised over the 60-minute scan, twin 2 EFW 20% larger than twin 1, both twins with normal umbilical artery Doppler and normal middle cerebral artery Doppler, and normal ductus venosus Doppler in both twins. There is no evidence of fetal hydrops. She has no contractions, no bleeding, cervix is 34 mm on transvaginal ultrasound. She lives 3 hours drive from the nearest fetal therapy centre.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, twin 1 fetal HR 148, twin 2 fetal HR 152
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound monochorionic diamniotic twins, twin 1 DVP 2 cm with bladder not visualised for 60 minutes (donor), twin 2 DVP 12 cm (recipient), EFW discordance 20%, umbilical artery Doppler normal both twins, MCA Doppler normal both twins, ductus venosus Doppler normal both twins, no hydrops, cervix 34 mm
data_table.History: Primigravida, monochorionic diamniotic twins confirmed at 12 weeks, 3-hour drive from fetal therapy centre, no contractions or bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently today to a national fetal therapy centre for consideration of fetoscopic laser photocoagulation
Perform therapeutic amnioreduction at the local hospital and continue serial ultrasound assessments every 2 weeks
Recommend expectant management with weekly ultrasound and no intervention until Doppler indices become abnormal
Discuss selective feticide of the donor twin now as the preferred first-line intervention at this gestation
Plan urgent delivery this week by caesarean section given the current Quintero staging and gestational age

subtopic_detail: New pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old primigravida at 34+2 weeks referred by her midwife for elevated blood pressure of 168/108 mmHg on two readings 15 minutes apart. She reports a frontal headache since morning and one episode of epigastric discomfort. There is no visual disturbance, no vaginal bleeding, and normal fetal movements. She has no prior hypertension, no chronic kidney disease, and no significant family history. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein and she has bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin. Fetal heart rate is 148 with reactive CTG.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 168/108, pulse 92, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Urine: protein/creatinine ratio 82 mg/mmol (<30), no blood, no leukocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give IV labetalol 20 mg bolus, load magnesium sulfate 4 g IV, admit for delivery within 24 to 48 hours
Start oral labetalol 200 mg 12-hourly, admit for expectant management with twice weekly review
Perform an immediate category-1 caesarean section without acute BP control given severe hypertension present
Discharge home with sublingual nifedipine 10 mg as required and midwife visit tomorrow morning for repeat BP
Give IV furosemide 40 mg for oedema and start oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily as monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Aspirin prophylaxis for pre-eclampsia
stem: You are the GP obstetric shared-care doctor reviewing a 34-year-old G2P1 at her booking visit at 10+3 weeks. Her previous pregnancy was complicated by pre-eclampsia at 33 weeks requiring preterm delivery. She has chronic hypertension controlled on labetalol 200 mg twice daily and a BMI of 33. She has no bleeding disorder, no aspirin allergy, and no history of peptic ulcer disease. She is a non-smoker. Her BP today is 132/84 with urine dipstick clear.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 132/84, pulse 78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, weight 88 kg
data_table.History: Previous PET at 33 weeks, chronic HTN on labetalol, BMI 33, no aspirin allergy, no peptic ulcer
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (110-140), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 umol/L (45-90), no proteinuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic recommendation?

options.text: Defer aspirin until 20+0 weeks when placental circulation matures and start at a dose of 75 mg once daily
Start aspirin 150 mg oral at night from 12+0 weeks and continue until 36+0 weeks gestation completed
Prescribe elemental calcium 1.5 g daily as first-line prevention instead of aspirin due to safety profile
Advise conservative dietary sodium restriction to below 2 g per day and no pharmacological prophylaxis required
Prescribe enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily throughout pregnancy for placental insufficiency prevention

subtopic_detail: Moderate hyperemesis gravidarum
stem: You are the ED registrar assessing a 26-year-old primigravida at 9+2 weeks with 5 days of persistent vomiting and inability to tolerate oral intake. She has lost 3.8 kg (5.2 percent of pre-pregnancy weight). She has no abdominal pain, no fever, no diarrhoea, no vaginal bleeding, and no dysuria. Urinalysis shows 3+ ketones and specific gravity 1.030 with no leukocytes or nitrites. Bedside ultrasound confirms a live intrauterine pregnancy consistent with dates with no adnexal mass. She has already tried oral ginger with no benefit.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 96/62, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Na 133 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), Cl 92 mmol/L (95-110), urea 8.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 68 umol/L (45-90), venous pH 7.48, bicarbonate 30 mmol/L, urine ketones 3+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Discharge on oral pyridoxine 40 mg TDS plus doxylamine 25 mg nocte with GP review the following morning
Give IV 5 percent dextrose 1 L over one hour then metoclopramide 10 mg IV before considering discharge from ED
Admit for IV normal saline with added potassium and give thiamine 100 mg IV before any dextrose containing fluid
Start oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for two weeks as first-line steroid therapy for refractory presentation today
Order urgent MRI brain to exclude posterior fossa lesion before any antiemetic therapy is commenced overnight

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency in third trimester
stem: You are the antenatal clinic registrar seeing a 30-year-old G3P2 at 30+1 weeks referred with tiredness and a haemoglobin of 92 g/L on routine bloods. She has previously tried oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily for the past 4 weeks but describes intolerable epigastric pain and constipation and admits to non-adherence for the last 2 weeks. She has no bleeding, no chronic disease, and no known haemoglobinopathy. Iron studies confirm iron deficiency. Her booking Hb was 116 g/L and she has no thalassaemia trait. She is not Rh negative.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Bloods: Hb 92 g/L (110-140), MCV 74 fL (80-100), ferritin 8 ug/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 8 percent (20-40)
data_table.History: Failed oral ferrous sulfate (intolerance), 30+1 weeks, no bleeding, no haemoglobinopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Increase oral ferrous sulfate to 325 mg three times daily and add ascorbic acid 500 mg to enhance absorption
Refer for a two unit packed red blood cell transfusion this week to correct haemoglobin promptly for delivery
Recommend dietary iron increase alone with red meat, leafy greens, and legumes daily and repeat FBE at 36 weeks
Arrange a single IV ferric carboxymaltose infusion of 1000 mg over 15 minutes as an outpatient day case
Start intramuscular iron sucrose 200 mg daily for 5 doses at the local community pharmacy over the coming week

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic bacteriuria at 14 weeks
stem: You are the antenatal clinic doctor reviewing a 27-year-old primigravida at 14+2 weeks. Her routine midstream urine culture returned pure growth of Escherichia coli at 10^8 CFU/mL, sensitive to nitrofurantoin, cefalexin, trimethoprim, and amoxicillin. She has no urinary symptoms, no fever, no back pain, and no vaginal discharge. She has no drug allergies, no G6PD deficiency, no chronic kidney disease, and is not currently on any regular medications. She has never had a UTI before this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.MSU: E. coli 10^8 CFU/mL, sensitive nitrofurantoin, cefalexin, trimethoprim, amoxicillin
data_table.History: 14+2 weeks, no symptoms, no G6PD, no CKD, no allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?

options.text: Trimethoprim 300 mg orally daily for 3 days with folic acid 5 mg daily due to interference with folate metabolism
Fosfomycin 3 g single sachet orally taken on an empty stomach with 200 mL of water at bedtime for optimal effect
Wait for symptoms to develop before treating and repeat MSU at 20 weeks to confirm bacteriuria persists longer
Amoxicillin 500 mg orally 8-hourly for 5 days as first-line therapy because E. coli sensitivity is confirmed here
Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally 6-hourly for 5 days and repeat MSU 1 to 2 weeks after treatment

subtopic_detail: Complete molar pregnancy follow-up
stem: You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 25-year-old G1P0 following suction curettage yesterday for a confirmed complete hydatidiform mole diagnosed on ultrasound (snowstorm appearance) with a pre-operative beta hCG of 285,000 IU/L. Histology has confirmed complete mole. She is otherwise well, no bleeding, and observations are normal. She is not on any contraception and asks about future pregnancy plans. She reports her partner is very keen for a family soon.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 74, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: beta hCG 285000 IU/L pre-op, Hb 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 245 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: Preoperative USS: snowstorm appearance, no adnexal mass, no theca lutein cysts, empty uterus post-evacuation on today's scan

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up plan?

options.text: Serial serum beta hCG weekly until three negative results then monthly for 6 months, effective contraception advised
Discharge with GP follow-up if any bleeding recurs; no formal hCG monitoring required after evacuation is complete
