Start prophylactic methotrexate 50 mg IM weekly for 8 weeks as chemoprophylaxis to reduce recurrence risk
Insert copper intrauterine device today to provide long-acting reversible contraception during monitoring
Arrange staging CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis this week to exclude metastatic gestational trophoblastic neoplasia

subtopic_detail: Uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twins timing of delivery
stem: You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 32-year-old G2P1 at 34+0 weeks with an uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy. Fortnightly ultrasound surveillance since 16 weeks has shown concordant growth, normal Dopplers, no TTTS features, and both amniotic sacs with normal fluid volumes. Both twins are cephalic-cephalic. She is asymptomatic. She had a spontaneous vaginal delivery in her first pregnancy at term. She has no significant medical history and no contraindication to vaginal birth. Cervical length is 32 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Ultrasound today: Both twins cephalic, EFW 2100 g and 2150 g (concordant), normal Dopplers, no TTTS, AFI both sacs normal, cervix 32 mm
data_table.History: MCDA twins, uncomplicated, prior SVD at term, no medical comorbidity

lead_in: What is the recommended timing and mode of delivery?

options.text: Elective delivery at 36+0 to 36+6 weeks with vaginal birth if leading twin cephalic and no contraindications
Continue expectant management to 39+0 weeks and induce at that point if no spontaneous labour has yet occurred
Deliver by elective caesarean section at 37+0 weeks regardless of presentation because of monochorionicity alone
Elective delivery at 38+0 weeks by induction of labour matching the recommended timing for dichorionic twin sets
Elective delivery at 32+0 weeks with antenatal steroids and neonatal team present as monoamniotic protocol applies

subtopic_detail: Decreased fetal movements at 34 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 34+3 weeks who has attended day assessment because of reduced fetal movements over the past 12 hours; previously her baby was very active. She reports no bleeding, no leaking, no pain, and is otherwise well. She has no significant obstetric history and had normal 20 week anomaly ultrasound and normal growth scans. She has no medical comorbidity. Symphysis-fundal height is 34 cm.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non-tender, longitudinal lie, cephalic, SFH 34 cm, no bleeding
data_table.History: Decreased fetal movements 12 hours, otherwise well, 34+3 weeks, no risk factors

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Reassure and discharge home with fetal movement chart and advice to return if concerns persist next 24 hours
Continuous CTG for at least 20 minutes and arrange a growth and Doppler ultrasound within 24 hours
Arrange immediate category-1 caesarean section this hour on the basis of the maternal report alone without CTG
Advise a large sugary drink, lie on left side, and recount movements over 2 hours before any medical assessment
Empirical betamethasone dose today and elective induction of labour in 48 hours for suspected placental dysfunction

subtopic_detail: Rhesus D negative routine prophylaxis
stem: You are the antenatal clinic doctor reviewing a 24-year-old primigravida at 27+5 weeks. Her booking blood group is O RhD negative with a negative antibody screen. She has had no antenatal bleeding, no invasive procedures, and no external cephalic version. She has no other medical problems. Partner blood group is unknown. Her booking bloods are otherwise normal. She has no allergies to blood products and no previous exposure to anti-D immunoglobulin.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Booking bloods: Group O RhD negative, antibody screen negative, no sensitising events, no procedures
data_table.History: Primigravida, 27+5 weeks, no bleeding, partner group unknown, no prior anti-D exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D prophylaxis plan?

options.text: Give a single anti-D 1500 IU dose at 34 weeks only, with no antenatal dose earlier and no post-delivery dose
Only give anti-D post-delivery if baby is RhD positive; no antenatal prophylaxis if there is no sensitising event
Give anti-D 625 IU intramuscular at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks, plus at delivery if baby is RhD positive
Determine paternal RhD group first and withhold anti-D if the father is proven to be RhD negative on testing
Anti-D 250 IU intramuscular now and repeat every 4 weeks throughout pregnancy for maximum sensitisation prevention

subtopic_detail: Shoulder dystocia first-line manoeuvres
stem: You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite when a 32-year-old G3P2 at 40+2 weeks in spontaneous labour delivers the head of an appropriately grown baby but no restitution occurs and the head retracts against the perineum (turtle sign) with no further progress despite maternal effort during the next contraction. She had no gestational diabetes and estimated fetal weight was 3600 g. She has no known coagulopathy and epidural is in situ providing analgesia. There is no cord prolapse and CTG has been reassuring throughout.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Intrapartum: Full dilation reached 40 min ago, head delivered 30 seconds ago, turtle sign, no restitution
data_table.Fetal: Reassuring CTG until delivery of head, EFW 3600 g, no cord prolapse

lead_in: What is the correct first-line manoeuvre?

options.text: Immediate category-1 caesarean section after replacement of the head using the Zavanelli manoeuvre technique
Apply vigorous fundal pressure downward on the maternal abdomen at the height of the next uterine contraction
Perform immediate midline episiotomy first and pull firmly on the fetal head to complete delivery without further steps
Ask the mother to flex both hips and knees onto her abdomen (McRoberts position) and apply suprapubic pressure now
Start an oxytocin infusion to strengthen contractions and encourage additional pushing effort by the mother now

subtopic_detail: Cervical screening at age 25
stem: You are the GP seeing a 25-year-old woman for her first cervical screening test since turning 25. She is sexually active, has been vaccinated against HPV as a schoolgirl, has no abnormal bleeding, no post-coital bleeding, and no known immunosuppression. She has never had cervical screening before because she declined uptake at prior GP visits. She has no HIV, no transplant, and no chronic immunosuppressive therapy. She is not pregnant. She asks whether she can self-collect the sample.

data_table.History: 25 years old, HPV vaccinated, sexually active, no symptoms, first CST, no immunosuppression, not pregnant
data_table.Vital signs: unremarkable
data_table.Preference: Self-collection acceptable to patient if offered

lead_in: What is the most appropriate screening plan?

options.text: Perform a Pap smear cytology every 2 years from age 21 onwards continuing throughout the reproductive years
Test HPV plus reflex liquid-based cytology and continue every 12 months regardless of the first result obtained here
Screening is not required until age 30 because she has completed the HPV vaccination schedule as a schoolgirl
Colposcopy referral as the initial screening approach since she has never had any prior cervical screening test
Offer HPV self-collection or clinician-collected sample; if HPV negative next screen in 5 years' time

subtopic_detail: Heavy menstrual bleeding first-line therapy
stem: You are the GP seeing a 35-year-old woman with 12 months of heavy menstrual bleeding causing flooding on 3 to 4 days of each cycle, requiring 2-hourly pad change and passing clots. She has no intermenstrual bleeding, no post-coital bleeding, and no pelvic pain. Cervical screening is up to date and negative. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal-sized uterus with no fibroids, polyps, or endometrial thickening. FBE shows Hb 106 g/L with ferritin 12. She has completed her family (2 children), takes no medications, and has no VTE history. Bimanual examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Bloods: Hb 106 g/L (115-155 female), ferritin 12 ug/L (30-200), TSH normal, coagulation screen normal
data_table.Imaging: Pelvic USS: normal uterus, endometrial thickness 6 mm, no polyps, no fibroids, no ovarian mass
data_table.History: Family complete, no VTE, no smoking, no migraine with aura, cervical screening up to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line therapy?

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS 52 mg) as first-line therapy for heavy menstrual bleeding without structural cause
Endometrial ablation as first-line surgical management before any trial of medical or hormonal therapy is undertaken
Total abdominal hysterectomy as definitive treatment because it eliminates the possibility of recurrence entirely
Ferrous sulfate 325 mg oral daily and expectant management with review in 12 months when anaemia has resolved
GnRH agonist depot injection for 6 months to induce medical menopause followed by expectant observation only

subtopic_detail: Contraception initiation after birth
stem: You are the GP seeing a 30-year-old woman at 3 weeks postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery of her second child. She is exclusively breastfeeding and is going well with lactation. She wants effective contraception before returning to sexual activity. She has no VTE history, is a non-smoker, has BMI 26, no migraine, and no hypertension. Her preference is for a hormonal oral option rather than an intrauterine device. She is not experiencing depression symptoms.

data_table.History: 3 weeks postpartum, exclusive breastfeeding, previous SVD, no VTE, non-smoker, no migraine, BMI 26
data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 118/74, pulse 74
data_table.Preference: Oral hormonal contraception preferred over LARC or barrier

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill starting now to give effective ovulation suppression during breastfeeding period
Progestogen-only pill (POP) can start today; category 1 or 2 for breastfeeding at any time from 21 days postpartum
Barrier method only until 6 months postpartum and no hormonal contraceptive during exclusive breastfeeding period
Insert copper intrauterine device today at the GP appointment even though she has expressed preference for oral option
Depo-Provera injection today then combined oral contraceptive from 6 months postpartum after weaning is completed

subtopic_detail: Threatened miscarriage at 8 weeks with fetal heart present
stem: You are the GP seeing a 28-year-old primigravida at 8+3 weeks with 2 days of light painless per vaginal bleeding. Speculum shows a closed cervix and mild dark bleeding, no products of conception seen. She has no fever, no severe pain, and no dizziness. Transvaginal ultrasound today confirms an intrauterine pregnancy with a live embryo, CRL consistent with 8+2 weeks and fetal heart rate 154 bpm. She has no significant medical history and no Rh negative blood group. Vital signs are stable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Closed cervix, mild dark bleeding, no adnexal tenderness, no products seen
data_table.Ultrasound: IUP with live embryo CRL 8+2, FHR 154 bpm, no subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Empiric progesterone 400 mg pessary twice daily until 16 weeks as suggested by PRISM trial in every case here
Bed rest for 2 weeks with no work attendance and daily transvaginal ultrasound scans to monitor pregnancy status
Expectant management with return advice for increased bleeding, severe pain, or reduced pregnancy symptoms today
Suction curettage this afternoon to prevent progression to inevitable miscarriage and complete the pregnancy loss
Empirical anti-D immunoglobulin injection today because she has had per vaginal bleeding in first trimester

subtopic_detail: Vulvovaginal candidiasis in pregnancy
stem: You are the GP seeing a 27-year-old woman at 22+1 weeks with 4 days of vulval itch, thick white discharge, and superficial dysuria. Speculum reveals typical thick white curd-like discharge with erythema and no cervical motion tenderness. She has no fever, no pelvic pain, and no risk factors for STI. She has no known allergies and has no history of recurrent thrush. She has previously used oral fluconazole for the same symptoms outside of pregnancy without adverse effect. Point-of-care wet prep shows budding yeast; pH 4.2; no clue cells; no trichomonads.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema, thick white curd-like discharge, no CMT, no adnexal tenderness
data_table.Wet prep: Budding yeast present; pH 4.2; no clue cells; no trichomonads

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose repeated once after 72 hours as it worked previously without adverse effect
Oral itraconazole 200 mg twice daily for a single day and abstain from intercourse for one week completely
Intravaginal boric acid 600 mg pessary daily for 14 days as antimicrobial therapy in pregnancy for the itch
Clotrimazole 100 mg intravaginal pessary at night for 6 nights and clotrimazole 1 percent cream to vulva as needed
Betamethasone valerate 0.05 percent cream applied twice daily to the vulva for symptom relief as monotherapy today

subtopic_detail: Chronic hypertension in early pregnancy on ACE inhibitor
stem: You are the antenatal clinic doctor seeing a 34-year-old G2P1 at 8+2 weeks with chronic hypertension diagnosed 2 years ago. She has been taking perindopril 5 mg daily with good control. She reports BP is running 128/82 at home. She had a prior term delivery without complication before starting perindopril. She has no proteinuria, no cardiac or renal disease, and no other medications. She wants to know whether her medication is safe in pregnancy and whether it should continue.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 128/82, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.History: Chronic HTN 2 years on perindopril 5 mg, prior term SVD, no proteinuria, no CKD, no other meds
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 68 umol/L (45-90), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), no proteinuria on dipstick

lead_in: What is the most appropriate medication change?

options.text: Continue perindopril at the current dose because it is providing good BP control and pregnancy is well established
Continue perindopril in the first trimester and switch to labetalol at the start of the second trimester exposure
Stop perindopril and start hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg orally daily as first-line pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive
Stop perindopril and start atenolol 50 mg orally daily as long-term beta blocker for pregnancy-safe control
Stop perindopril today and start labetalol 100 mg orally twice daily titrated to BP with methyldopa alternative

subtopic_detail: Suspected choledocholithiasis at 26 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar consulted about a 30-year-old G1 at 26+3 weeks admitted with 3 days of right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and pale stools. She has no fever, no rigors, and remains haemodynamically stable. Bloods show cholestatic LFT rise with markedly raised bilirubin. Abdominal ultrasound shows a distended common bile duct 10 mm with a suspected distal stone; no acute cholecystitis; multiple small gallstones present in the gallbladder. She is not septic and observations are normal. She has no allergies and is on no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Imaging: CBD 10 mm distended, suspected distal stone, multiple gallstones in GB, no cholecystitis, no ductal dilatation intrahepatic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management step?

options.text: Arrange MRCP for diagnostic confirmation; if choledocholithiasis confirmed, proceed to ERCP with lead shielding
Proceed directly to open cholecystectomy and common bile duct exploration today under general anaesthesia
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast is the most appropriate first imaging to evaluate the biliary tree and stones
Conservative management with IV antibiotics and analgesia for 2 weeks until postpartum ERCP after birth
Immediate delivery by category-2 caesarean section to allow definitive surgical management of the biliary disease

subtopic_detail: Suspected uterine rupture during VBAC
stem: You are the on-call obstetric registrar attending a 34-year-old G2P1 with previous lower-segment caesarean section undergoing trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC) at 40+2 weeks. She is at 8 cm dilatation on epidural analgesia with an oxytocin augmentation running. She reports sudden severe suprapubic pain that persists between contractions. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration to 60 bpm sustained for 3 minutes. On abdominal examination, the presenting part is no longer felt at the previously reached station and there is fresh vaginal bleeding. She is haemodynamically borderline.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air
data_table.Intrapartum: Prior LSCS, 8 cm on oxytocin, sudden severe pain persisting between contractions, station lost, fresh PV bleed
data_table.Fetal: Prolonged deceleration to 60 bpm, no recovery for 3 minutes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue oxytocin at current rate and give tocolysis with terbutaline 250 mcg subcutaneously to relieve uterine hypertonus
Stop oxytocin, resuscitate with fluids and cross-match, arrange emergency category-1 laparotomy for suspected rupture
Perform urgent bedside ultrasound to rule out placental abruption before proceeding to any operative delivery decision
Attempt instrumental vaginal delivery with forceps to expedite delivery while operating theatre is being prepared for use
Give IV bolus antibiotic prophylaxis and observe for 30 minutes to see whether the CTG spontaneously recovers back

subtopic_detail: Suspected magnesium sulfate toxicity
stem: You are the on-call obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G2P1 at 36+4 weeks with severe pre-eclampsia commenced on IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose followed by an infusion at 1 g/hour 6 hours ago. She now reports blurred vision, generalised weakness, and difficulty in swallowing. Nursing staff report she has become drowsy in the last 15 minutes. Deep tendon reflexes are absent bilaterally. Respiratory rate is 8 per minute. She has a background of stage 2 CKD (creatinine 130 umol/L) that was known before admission. Urine output has been 15 mL over the last hour.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 62, blood pressure 152/94, respiratory rate 8, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, absent DTRs bilaterally, diaphragmatic weakness on inspection, oliguria
data_table.Bloods: creatinine 158 umol/L (from baseline 130), potassium 4.4, magnesium level pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue magnesium at current rate and give naloxone 400 mcg IV to reverse suspected opioid respiratory depression cause
Increase IV fluid rate to 250 mL/hour and continue magnesium at reduced 0.5 g/hour rate for continued PET prophylaxis
Stop the magnesium infusion, give 10 percent calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 10 minutes, and check serum magnesium
Give IV furosemide 40 mg to increase magnesium excretion and reduce serum level over the next 2 to 4 hours
Initiate haemodialysis with vascular access placed via femoral vein this hour for magnesium removal from bloodstream

subtopic_detail: Retained placenta at 45 minutes with brisk bleeding
stem: You are the obstetric registrar attending a 28-year-old G3P2 at 40+1 weeks who delivered vaginally 45 minutes ago after active management of the third stage (oxytocin 10 units IM given, controlled cord traction attempted). The placenta remains undelivered, cord traction has been unsuccessful, and there is now brisk PV bleeding estimated at 800 mL. The uterus is deviated to the right and feels boggy. She has a functioning epidural in situ from labour. She is haemodynamically stable but observations are trending toward tachycardia. IV access is patent with a 16 gauge cannula and cross-match sent.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Uterus deviated right, boggy on palpation, cord in situ, brisk PV bleeding, placenta not delivered
data_table.Third stage: 45 min elapsed, oxytocin 10 U IM given, CCT unsuccessful, estimated 800 mL blood loss

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give an intraumbilical vein injection of oxytocin 20 units in 20 mL saline via the placental cord to deliver the placenta
Wait another 30 minutes for spontaneous separation while giving IM ergometrine to encourage delivery of the placenta
Perform bimanual uterine compression and give a further oxytocin 10 units IM before considering surgical intervention
Empty the bladder, transfer to theatre for manual removal under spinal or epidural top-up, IV oxytocin infusion, and give prophylactic antibiotics
Proceed to emergency subtotal hysterectomy as definitive haemorrhage control since manual removal has not been attempted

subtopic_detail: Aspirin failure with new severe pre-eclampsia at 32 weeks
stem: You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 36-year-old G3P1 (with a prior pre-eclampsia and prior stillbirth at 34 weeks) at 32+1 weeks. She has been on aspirin 150 mg from 13 weeks. She has developed BP of 172/112 mmHg, severe headache, and epigastric pain over 24 hours. Bloods show a rapid rise in creatinine and low platelets. Urine protein/creatinine ratio is 350 mg/mmol. CTG is currently reactive. She has no HELLP features on LFTs. Estimated fetal weight is 1650 g on today's ultrasound.

data_table.Vital signs: blood pressure 172/112, pulse 96, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L, platelets 95 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 108 umol/L (from baseline 68), ALT 42 U/L (<35), LDH 245 U/L (135-225), urate 0.48 mmol/L (0.15-0.35)
data_table.Fetal: CTG reactive, EFW 1650 g, umbilical Doppler normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Discharge on oral labetalol 400 mg TDS with community midwife review every 3 days until symptoms improve here
Continue expectant management with weekly clinic review until 37 weeks then induce labour if symptoms have resolved
Emergency category-1 caesarean section within 30 minutes without acute BP control or magnesium sulfate loading first
Stop aspirin immediately as it has failed to prevent pre-eclampsia and start high-dose prednisolone 40 mg orally daily
IV labetalol 20 mg (repeat every 10 min), IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, deliver in 24 to 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Vasa praevia with bleed at 32 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit for a 32-year-old woman at 32+3 weeks who has a small volume of bright red vaginal bleeding after a bowel motion. She had a second trimester scan reporting a low-lying velamentous cord insertion with a vessel crossing the internal os, confirmed on transvaginal imaging at 26 weeks. She is not contracting. Membranes are intact. Cardiotocograph shows a baseline of 145 with normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations. Speculum shows a small amount of fresh blood at the cervix, os closed.

She has completed one course of betamethasone at 28 weeks for a prior bleed. She is haemodynamically stable and asking whether she can go home given the bleeding has stopped.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Bloods: Hb 116 g/L (110-140), platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400), Kleihauer negative, group and hold on file
data_table.Imaging: confirmed vasa praevia with vessel over internal os, cord insertion velamentous, placental edge 3 cm from os

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Discharge home with twice weekly CTG and outpatient scan, plan caesarean at 39 weeks after any further bleed
Admit until delivery, give a second course of betamethasone, plan elective caesarean at 34 to 35 weeks
Perform an immediate category-1 caesarean now because any bleeding with vasa praevia is a fetal emergency
Admit for observation for 48 hours then discharge if no further bleeding, plan vaginal delivery at 37 weeks
Discharge with prescribed magnesium sulfate at home for neuroprotection and plan caesarean at 36 weeks

subtopic_detail: Early-onset severe FGR with absent end-diastolic flow at 30 weeks
stem:
You are the maternal-fetal medicine registrar assessing a 34-year-old primigravida at 30+1 weeks with a small-for-gestational-age fetus first noted at the 28-week scan. Her repeat growth scan today shows estimated fetal weight less than the third centile, abdominal circumference less than the third centile, and umbilical artery Doppler showing absent end-diastolic flow across three consecutive cycles. Middle cerebral artery pulsatility index is at the fifth centile with a cerebroplacental ratio of 0.9. Amniotic fluid index is 6 cm. Ductus venosus a-wave is present and positive.

Her blood pressure is 128/82, urine dipstick shows no protein. Cardiotocograph is reactive with normal variability. She has completed a course of betamethasone at 28 weeks. Bloods including bile acids and pre-eclampsia screen are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78, blood pressure 128/82, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 152
data_table.Doppler: UA absent end-diastolic flow, MCA PI 5th centile, CPR 0.9, DV a-wave positive
data_table.Growth: EFW <3rd centile, AC <3rd centile, HC 10th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step now?

options.text: Continue outpatient weekly Doppler until 34 weeks then deliver by planned caesarean with corticosteroid cover
Deliver by category-2 caesarean today after magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection because absent EDF alone at 30 weeks mandates delivery
Admit for daily CTG plus twice weekly Doppler surveillance and plan delivery at 32 weeks if ductus venosus a-wave becomes absent or reversed
Give a second course of betamethasone now and induce labour with vaginal prostaglandin for delivery within 48 hours
Start low-dose aspirin and prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin to improve placental perfusion, review in a week

subtopic_detail: Impacted fetal head at full dilation caesarean
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar taking a category-1 caesarean for a 32-year-old at 39+4 weeks who has been fully dilated for two hours and pushing for 90 minutes. Fetal head is at spines +2 in the occipito-posterior position, cephalic. She has been contracting strongly. A cardiotocograph shows a prolonged deceleration to 60 for 5 minutes despite scalp stimulation and stopping oxytocin.

In theatre you make a lower segment transverse incision but find the fetal head deeply impacted in the pelvis and cannot dislodge it with the operator's fingers from above. An assistant attempts to push the head up from below via the vagina without success. Two minutes have passed since delivery of the incision.

data_table.Vital signs: maternal pulse 108, blood pressure 132/78, SpO2 99% on room air, fetal heart rate 60 (prolonged deceleration)
data_table.Progress: second stage 2 hours, active pushing 90 minutes, station spines +2, OP position, caput++, moulding++
data_table.Operative: lower segment transverse uterine incision made, head impacted deep in pelvis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Administer terbutaline 250 micrograms subcutaneously to relax the uterus and reattempt head disimpaction
Extend the lower segment incision inferiorly with scissors to allow more room and deliver the head with forceps
Ask the assistant to push harder from below using the whole hand until the head disimpacts and can be delivered abdominally
Deliver the fetus by reverse breech extraction, grasping a foot and delivering as breech through the abdominal incision
Perform a classical vertical uterine incision above the impacted head and deliver by rotating the fetus in utero

subtopic_detail: Suspected amniotic fluid embolism intrapartum
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called for a woman who has collapsed on the labour ward. She is a 34-year-old at 39+6 weeks who had artificial rupture of membranes 15 minutes ago for augmentation. Immediately afterwards she developed sudden severe shortness of breath, complained of feeling terrified, and lost consciousness. She had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds.

She is now on oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreather, blood pressure 65/32, pulse 148 with peripheral cyanosis, oxygen saturations 84 percent, CTG shows fetal bradycardia at 60 bpm. The airway is patent. Her uterus is soft with a trickle of dark blood from the vagina that is not clotting on the drape.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 148, blood pressure 65/32, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 84% on 15 L/min, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 60
data_table.Recent event: ARM 15 minutes ago, sudden dyspnoea, seizure 90 seconds, now unconscious
data_table.Bleeding: trickle of non-clotting dark blood per vaginam, uterus soft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management sequence?

options.text: Perform an urgent bedside echocardiogram before initiating any treatment to confirm right heart strain and pulmonary embolism
Give IV magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus for seizure control then plan urgent caesarean under general anaesthesia
Give tranexamic acid 1 g IV and syntocinon infusion 40 units in 500 mL, transfer directly to theatre for caesarean
Administer IM adrenaline 0.5 mg for suspected anaphylaxis to latex or antibiotics and observe for response
Call arrest team, secure airway with CPR if pulseless, activate massive transfusion, and prepare perimortem caesarean by 4 minutes if no ROSC

subtopic_detail: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy with severe bile acids
stem:
You are the antenatal registrar reviewing a 32-year-old primigravida at 36+1 weeks referred by her GP with two weeks of intense generalised itch worse at night, particularly on palms and soles, no rash. She has no jaundice, no right upper quadrant pain, and no history of hepatobiliary disease.

Her bloods show total bile acids 118 micromol/L (fasting reference less than 10 micromol/L), ALT 168 U/L (less than 35), bilirubin 22 micromol/L (less than 21), gamma-GT 34 U/L (less than 45). Coagulation is normal. Fetal movements are perceived normally and CTG this morning is reactive with normal variability. Estimated fetal weight is on the 45th centile. Hepatitis screen and autoimmune liver screen are negative.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: bile acids 118 micromol/L (<10), ALT 168 U/L (<35), bilirubin 22 micromol/L (<21), gamma-GT 34 U/L (<45), INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily and continue conservative management until 39 weeks for spontaneous labour
Plan induction of labour at 35 to 36 weeks now because bile acids over 100 micromol/L confer a marked stillbirth risk from 36 weeks
Perform an urgent category-1 caesarean today because bile acids over 100 mandate immediate delivery
Give a course of antenatal betamethasone and plan expectant management with weekly CTG until 38 weeks
Prescribe rifampicin 300 mg twice daily to reduce itch and defer delivery until 39 weeks after normal weekly Doppler surveillance

subtopic_detail: Acute uterine inversion at third stage
stem:
You are the labour ward registrar called for a woman collapsed after vaginal delivery. She is a 30-year-old para 2 who delivered a 4.1 kg baby 5 minutes ago. The midwife applied controlled cord traction to deliver the placenta but immediately noted the woman becoming pale and tachycardic. On examination the woman is diaphoretic and confused. On abdominal palpation the uterine fundus is no longer palpable. A dark red vascular mass is visible protruding from the vagina with the placenta attached. There is heavy bleeding.

An 18-gauge IV is in situ, syntocinon 10 units IM has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Exam: fundus non-palpable abdominally, red vascular mass at introitus with placenta attached, heavy bleeding
data_table.Access: 18-gauge IV in right hand, syntocinon 10 units IM given post-delivery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Immediately replace the fundus with a cupped hand (Johnson manoeuvre) leaving placenta attached, then remove placenta after reduction
Remove the placenta manually first because retained placenta perpetuates the inversion, then attempt fundal replacement
Start an oxytocin infusion of 40 units in 500 mL to contract the uterus and stop the bleeding, then attempt reduction after 15 minutes
Insert a Bakri balloon into the visible inverted mass and inflate with 500 mL saline for uterine tamponade of bleeding
Transfer directly to theatre for immediate laparotomy and Huntington procedure without any attempt at vaginal reduction

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal bleeding with thickened endometrium
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 62-year-old woman referred by her GP with three episodes of light postmenopausal vaginal bleeding over the past six weeks. She is 12 years postmenopausal, has never used hormone replacement therapy, and has a body mass index of 34. She has hypertension on ramipril and type 2 diabetes on metformin. Her cervical screening is up to date and normal. Pelvic examination shows an atrophic vulva and vagina, cervix appears normal, small amount of old blood in the vault, no adnexal masses.

A transvaginal ultrasound today shows an endometrial thickness of 8 mm with heterogenous echo pattern and increased vascularity on colour Doppler. Ovaries are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 138/86, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Ultrasound: endometrial thickness 8 mm, heterogenous echotexture, increased vascularity on Doppler, ovaries normal
data_table.History: 62 years, BMI 34, T2DM, never HRT, cervical screening current and normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Perform outpatient Pipelle sampling in clinic and manage further only if malignancy is found on that specimen
Repeat the transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to see whether the endometrial thickness changes before proceeding to biopsy
Arrange hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy under general or local anaesthesia to sample the endometrium histologically
Start topical oestrogen for atrophic vaginitis and review symptoms in 8 weeks before further investigation
Arrange staging CT abdomen and pelvis and cancer antigen 125 to assess for advanced malignancy first

subtopic_detail: Complex adnexal mass with elevated risk of malignancy index
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 58-year-old woman with three months of increasing abdominal distension and early satiety. She is 8 years postmenopausal and has no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Abdominal examination reveals mild ascites and a palpable pelvic mass. On bimanual examination the mass is fixed, irregular, and non-tender.

A transvaginal and transabdominal ultrasound shows a 9 cm right adnexal mass with solid and cystic components, thick septations greater than 3 mm, papillary projections, and increased vascularity. There is a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum CA-125 is 320 kU/L (below 35). Her Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) is well above 200.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 128/80, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Ultrasound: right adnexal mass 9 cm, solid and cystic, septations >3 mm, papillary projections, vascular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange oral tranexamic acid and repeat imaging in 6 weeks to observe for change before intervention
Arrange percutaneous ultrasound-guided biopsy of the mass to obtain histological diagnosis before referral
Perform a diagnostic laparoscopy locally with washings and biopsies to establish diagnosis before onward referral
Refer to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team for planned surgery in a specialist centre with staging capability
Commence neoadjuvant carboplatin and paclitaxel and refer at completion for interval debulking

subtopic_detail: MRI-confirmed increta with planned delivery timing
stem:
You are the obstetric consultant reviewing a 36-year-old G4P3 at 33+0 weeks with two prior caesareans and an anterior placenta praevia. Ultrasound at 28 weeks showed multiple placental lakes, loss of the retroplacental clear zone, and bridging vessels crossing the bladder wall. MRI at 32 weeks confirms placenta increta with focal areas suspicious for percreta into the posterior bladder. She is asymptomatic today but reports a single small self-limited PV spot last week. The tertiary maternal-fetal medicine unit and interventional radiology are available on site.

She asks about the safest timing and mode of delivery given her prior counselling that she wants no further pregnancies.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 120/74, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 142
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 235 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 4.2 g/L (3.7-6.2), group and crossmatch 4 units on standby
data_table.Imaging: MRI increta with focal percreta signs into posterior bladder, no fetal growth restriction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Elective caesarean hysterectomy at 34+0 to 35+0 weeks in a specialist MDT theatre with IR standby
Expectant care to 37+0 weeks then elective caesarean with attempted placental removal in the local unit
Induce vaginal birth at 34+0 weeks after corticosteroids because the placenta may separate spontaneously later
Elective classical caesarean at 36+0 weeks with placenta left in situ and outpatient methotrexate follow-up
Emergency category-1 caesarean today because a single antepartum bleed indicates imminent placental separation

subtopic_detail: Recurrent early pregnancy loss with confirmed APS in the current pregnancy
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar seeing a 33-year-old G4P0 at 8+2 weeks. She has had three consecutive first trimester miscarriages between 6 and 9 weeks. Non-pregnant workup showed persistently positive lupus anticoagulant on two occasions 12 weeks apart, negative anticardiolipin and negative beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies. She has no personal history of venous thromboembolism and no systemic lupus features. Her current pregnancy is confirmed viable on ultrasound with a fetal heart rate of 142.

She is asking what treatment during this pregnancy will maximise her chance of a live birth.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 76, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 128 g/L (110-140), platelets 224 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 62 umol/L (45-90), APTT prolonged and not correcting on mixing (lupus anticoagulant pattern)
data_table.Imaging: single intrauterine pregnancy 8+2 weeks, cardiac activity present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for this pregnancy?

options.text: Therapeutic dose enoxaparin twice daily plus aspirin plus hydroxychloroquine for the whole pregnancy
Low dose aspirin 100 mg daily alone with no anticoagulant, reserving heparin for prior VTE only
Low dose aspirin 100 mg daily started now plus prophylactic dose enoxaparin daily throughout pregnancy
Warfarin bridged with enoxaparin from 12 weeks to term to prevent placental thrombosis in APS
Prednisolone 20 mg daily plus low dose aspirin from now until 20 weeks then wean and continue aspirin

subtopic_detail: Severe hypertension 190/125 with seizure prophylaxis before delivery at 35 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite reviewing a 29-year-old G2P1 at 35+0 weeks who arrived with a headache and one episode of vomiting. Blood pressure on two readings 15 minutes apart is 192/126. She has a normal reflex examination with no clonus. Fetal CTG shows a baseline of 148 with reduced variability but no decelerations. Her booking pressure was 118/72. Her platelets are 96 and her ALT is 128. Proteinuria is 3 plus on dipstick.

The consultant is on their way and has agreed to birth by caesarean today. You must start the medical priorities now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 192/126, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: Hb 108 g/L (110-140), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 128 U/L (5-40), creatinine 92 umol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.35), fibrinogen 3.8 g/L (3.7-6.2)
data_table.Imaging: cephalic presentation on portable ultrasound, estimated fetal weight 2450 g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral methyldopa 500 mg loading dose plus oral clonidine and admit for observation and 6 hourly reassessment
Immediate caesarean under general anaesthetic before any antihypertensive or magnesium sulfate is started
IV furosemide 40 mg to offload preload plus sublingual nifedipine because renal function is deteriorating
IV labetalol 20 mg bolus now with repeat dosing plus magnesium sulfate 4 g IV load then 1 g per hour
Phenytoin 15 mg per kg IV load for seizure prophylaxis, then transfer for caesarean when blood pressure settles

subtopic_detail: Severe grade with ascites and haemoconcentration after IVF retrieval
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old woman in ED, day 6 after IVF oocyte retrieval with 22 eggs collected. She reports progressive abdominal distension, nausea, reduced urine output, and dyspnoea on lying flat. Examination shows a tense abdomen with dullness to flank percussion, respiratory rate 24, and mild bilateral pitting oedema. She has no fever or vaginal bleeding. She had a fresh embryo transfer two days ago and a positive pregnancy test today. She is on no anticoagulant.

Her fertility unit clinician has asked for admission and initial management.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 108/72, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 168 g/L (110-140), haematocrit 0.52 (0.35-0.45), white cells 16.2 x10^9/L (4-11), creatinine 118 umol/L (45-90), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0)
data_table.Imaging: large volume ascites on bedside ultrasound, enlarged ovaries 9 cm bilateral, small right pleural effusion on chest X-ray

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start IV albumin infusion 25 percent 100 mL 6 hourly as sole volume expander plus oral fluid restriction
Discharge on oral fluids and outpatient follow up because ongoing pregnancy will resolve OHSS spontaneously
Give IV furosemide 40 mg to relieve dyspnoea and ascites, hold anticoagulation until diuresis achieved
Emergency laparotomy for ovarian decompression and drainage of ascites in theatre under general anaesthetic
Admit for IV crystalloid replacement, prophylactic enoxaparin daily, strict fluid balance, and paracentesis if symptomatic

subtopic_detail: 45 minute retention with heavy bleeding requiring theatre manual removal
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite 45 minutes after a normal vaginal birth of a 3200 g infant at term. Active management was used with oxytocin 10 units IM at delivery. The placenta remains undelivered and controlled cord traction has not succeeded. Estimated blood loss is now 900 mL and ongoing. The woman is haemodynamically borderline with a pulse of 108 and blood pressure 102/64. She has a spinal already sited. The consultant is 15 minutes away. Bladder was catheterised at delivery.

The theatre coordinator confirms an emergency theatre is ready.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 102/64, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Bloods: Hb 96 g/L (110-140), platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400), fibrinogen 3.2 g/L (3.7-6.2), 4 units red cells and 2 units FFP on standby
data_table.Imaging: no separation signs, cord in situ, empty bladder confirmed on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer to theatre now for manual removal of placenta under spinal top-up with syntocinon 40 units IV in 500 mL
Give ergometrine 250 mcg IM at the bedside and continue attempted cord traction for another 30 minutes
Attempt umbilical vein oxytocin injection of 30 units in saline at the bedside instead of theatre transfer
Insert a Bakri balloon vaginally and inflate to 500 mL to tamponade bleeding before removing the placenta
Wait one further hour with slow oxytocin infusion and no other intervention because delivery is common by 2 hours

subtopic_detail: PPROM at 32 weeks without infection, timing of delivery
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 28-year-old G2P1 admitted with PPROM at 32+2 weeks confirmed on speculum pooling and positive amnisure. She is 24 hours in with no contractions. Maternal observations are normal, CTG is reactive, and there are no clinical signs of chorioamnionitis. She has completed betamethasone 24 hours ago and is on oral erythromycin. Group B strep swab is pending.

She asks how long she should stay pregnant and what will trigger delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 138
data_table.Bloods: Hb 116 g/L (110-140), white cells 10.8 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 8 mg/L (under 5), platelets 244 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: cephalic presentation, deepest vertical pool 1.6 cm, normal Doppler indices

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Expectant care with inpatient surveillance until 37+0 weeks then induction of labour if not already delivered
Expectant care with inpatient surveillance to 36+0 weeks then plan delivery, sooner if infection or fetal distress
Induce labour today at 32+3 weeks because further latency increases sepsis risk beyond neonatal benefit
Discharge home with weekly clinic review and instructions on symptom monitoring for infection or bleeding
Start tocolysis with nifedipine and give a second course of betamethasone to prolong latency to 39 weeks

subtopic_detail: Second trimester dilatation with prolapsed membranes at 22 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 32-year-old G3P0 at 22+3 weeks who presents with painless pressure. Speculum shows cervix dilated to 3 cm with membranes hourglassing into the vagina. She has no bleeding, no contractions, and no fever. She had a mid-trimester loss at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy and a preterm birth at 26 weeks in her second. There is no evidence of infection on blood tests. Fetal biometry is normal for gestation.

She asks whether anything can prolong the pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/76, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius, fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: Hb 118 g/L (110-140), white cells 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 8 mg/L (under 5), platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Imaging: single viable fetus 22+3 weeks, cephalic, cervix funnelled with membranes prolapsed into vagina, normal Doppler

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate delivery at 22+3 weeks after magnesium neuroprotection because prognosis is otherwise dismal
Vaginal progesterone 200 mg nightly and expectant care because cerclage is contraindicated after cervical dilation
Offer rescue cervical cerclage under regional anaesthetic after counselling on risks and prognosis today
Arabin pessary placement alone with outpatient review at the local unit and no admission or antibiotics
Give IV magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection and antibiotics but no cerclage because membranes are prolapsed

subtopic_detail: Painless bleed at 32 weeks with an unknown placental site
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in an outer metropolitan hospital reviewing a 33-year-old G3P2 at 32 plus 3 weeks who presents with a single episode of painless bright red vaginal bleeding of around 200 mL after intercourse 1 hour ago. She has no contractions and reports normal fetal movements. Her booking ultrasound at 20 weeks reported a low placenta but a follow-up scan was cancelled by the patient. Blood group is O positive and no antibodies. Her previous births were vaginal at term with no complications.

On arrival she is calm and haemodynamically stable and the CTG is reassuring.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.9
data_table.Abdominal examination: soft non-tender uterus, fetus longitudinal with cephalic presentation, no palpable contractions
data_table.CTG: baseline 140, moderate variability, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140 pregnancy), platelets 232 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 5.1 g/L, group and hold sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial assessment step?

options.text: Perform a gentle bimanual digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation before any imaging
Give a stat course of steroids with IV oxytocin infusion to induce labour and expedite delivery given the bleed
Arrange transabdominal followed by transvaginal ultrasound to locate the placenta before any digital examination
Perform an urgent Kleihauer-Betke test and administer anti-D within the next 4 hours before proceeding to imaging
Discharge home once bleeding stops as the CTG is reassuring and she has stable observations at present time

subtopic_detail: OGTT cut-offs at 24-28 weeks and treatment escalation
stem:
You are the antenatal registrar reviewing a 34-year-old G2P1 at 27 plus 2 weeks in a suburban tertiary hospital antenatal clinic. She had gestational diabetes controlled with diet alone in her first pregnancy and delivered a 4.1 kg baby at term. Her booking BMI is 31. She has completed a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test 4 days ago. She is otherwise well and taking pregnancy multivitamins and iodine. She has no known thyroid disease and no family history of type 1 diabetes.

Her capillary fasting sugar this morning was 4.9 mmol/L.

data_table.OGTT (75 g): fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1), 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L (<10.0), 2 hour 8.1 mmol/L (<8.5)
data_table.Ultrasound (26 weeks): estimated fetal weight 70th centile, normal liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure her the OGTT is within normal limits and no gestational diabetes intervention is required at this time
Diagnose gestational diabetes and commence dietary review and 4 times daily self monitoring of blood glucose
Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately as first-line pharmacotherapy for gestational diabetes
Commence long-acting insulin glargine 10 units nocte immediately given the previous large baby history and BMI
Repeat the 75 g OGTT at 32 weeks with random blood glucose in between to confirm diagnosis is accurate

subtopic_detail: Uterotonic escalation after atony with a bleeding volume over 1.5 L
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the birth suite for a 29-year-old G1P1 who delivered a 4.0 kg male vaginally 25 minutes ago after a 90 minute second stage requiring vacuum assistance for maternal exhaustion. Estimated blood loss is 1.5 L and continues briskly. Bimanual compression is being maintained by the senior midwife. The placenta was delivered complete on the placenta tray. The uterus feels soft and boggy above the umbilicus. She has a history of essential hypertension on lifestyle measures only, controlled at booking.

IV oxytocin 10 units has been given and a further infusion is running.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Access: two large bore IVs, warm crystalloid running, cross-match sent
data_table.Uterine tone: soft, boggy above umbilicus despite bimanual compression
data_table.Prior medication: IV oxytocin 10 units bolus given, oxytocin infusion running at 40 mU/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic step?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 micrograms and repeat the dose in 15 minutes if the uterus remains atonic
Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device immediately as the second line uterotonic escalation therapy step
IM carboprost 250 micrograms and IV tranexamic acid 1 g with a second dose in 30 minutes if bleeding continues
Give sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms as the next line agent while awaiting theatre transfer arrangements
Transfer to theatre immediately for hysterectomy given the ongoing bleeding despite the uterotonic given so far

subtopic_detail: Emerging chorioamnionitis at 30 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 27-year-old G1P0 at 30 plus 4 weeks who was admitted 4 days ago after confirmed preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. She has completed a course of betamethasone and is on oral erythromycin. Today she reports mild lower abdominal discomfort intermittently and offensive smelling liquor since this morning. Fetal movements are reduced compared to yesterday. She has no vaginal bleeding.

Her temperature has risen this shift; the midwife has just recorded a further rise now.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4, fetal heart rate 172
data_table.Abdomen: uterus soft, palpable irregular contractions 1 in 10 minutes with mild tenderness
data_table.CTG: baseline 172, minimal variability, no decelerations, no accelerations for 30 minutes
data_table.Bloods: white cell count 18.6 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0 pregnancy), CRP 84 mg/L (<5), lactate 2.6 mmol/L (<2)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Continue oral erythromycin, hydrate with IV fluid, and add IV paracetamol with reassessment in 4 hours
Commence IV broad spectrum antibiotics and expedite delivery with neonatal team standby for the delivery event
Give a second course of betamethasone and plan tocolysis with nifedipine to reach 32 weeks before delivery is planned
Perform an urgent amniocentesis to obtain amniotic fluid culture before deciding on delivery timing today
Discharge home with oral amoxicillin and clindamycin and daily antenatal review until 34 weeks completed for delivery

subtopic: Pre-eclampsia superimposed on chronic kidney disease
subtopic_detail: Diagnosis when baseline proteinuria confounds standard cut-offs
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 35-year-old G2P1 at 33 plus 2 weeks with known IgA nephropathy and baseline proteinuria of around 500 mg per 24 hours pre-pregnancy on losartan (ceased pre-pregnancy). Her booking BP was 128/82. Today her BP is repeatedly 156/104 and she reports 2 days of frontal headache and blurring on the peripheries of vision. She has right upper quadrant discomfort and mild ankle swelling. Her creatinine baseline was 92 micromol/L pre-pregnancy.

Her partner has cared for their first child at home and asks whether she must stay in hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 158/104 (repeated 156/102), respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.8, fetal heart rate 148
data_table.Bloods: haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140), platelets 122 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 118 micromol/L (baseline 92), ALT 68 U/L (<40), urate 0.42 mmol/L (<0.36)
data_table.Urine: protein-to-creatinine ratio 92 mg/mmol (baseline 55, threshold for pre-eclampsia >30)
data_table.Fetal: estimated fetal weight 15th centile, growth crossing centiles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Give a course of steroids for fetal lung maturity and defer delivery until 37 weeks to reach term status
Restart losartan for baseline renal protection alongside oral labetalol 200 mg twice daily and outpatient BP diary
Give oral prazosin 500 micrograms three times daily as blood pressure control while continuing routine antenatal visits
Discharge home with 4 hourly self BP monitoring and daily fetal movements diary and specialist review in 48 hours
Admit for oral nifedipine 20 mg immediate release, IV magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis, and delivery planning

subtopic_detail: Suspicion during spontaneous rupture with fetal distress
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a busy labour ward. A 32-year-old G2P1 at 38 plus 3 weeks with a known velamentous cord insertion on 20 week ultrasound is in early labour at 3 cm dilated. The midwife has just performed an artificial rupture of membranes given inadequate contractions on syntocinon; there is a moderate amount of dark red blood immediately noted with the fluid. The CTG which was previously reassuring now shows sinusoidal pattern with baseline 100. Her observations are stable.

The attending consultant is scrubbed in theatre with another patient.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 120/70, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9, fetal HR 100 sinusoidal
data_table.Blood loss: moderate bright red with fluid at ARM, ongoing
data_table.Access: IV in situ with crystalloid running
data_table.Prior imaging: velamentous cord insertion documented at 20 weeks, no repeat targeted vasa praevia scan performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give an IV tranexamic acid 1 g bolus and IV fluid resuscitation to control maternal bleeding source volume
Stop syntocinon and reposition mother left lateral with oxygen by facemask and reassess CTG in 15 minutes
Take an Apt test on the vaginal blood specimen to determine whether the blood is maternal or fetal in origin
Perform an urgent transvaginal ultrasound to demonstrate vessel over the internal os before mobilising theatre
Prepare for immediate category 1 caesarean section under general anaesthesia while continuously monitoring fetal heart

subtopic: Postpartum haemorrhage with placenta accreta spectrum
subtopic_detail: Unexpected accreta at caesarean in a Jehovah's Witness declining blood products
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a regional tertiary hospital assisting a category 2 caesarean at 38 weeks in a 38-year-old G4P3 with 2 previous caesareans and a documented low-lying anterior placenta. During delivery of the placenta there is dense adherence, unresponsive to gentle traction; there is now torrential haemorrhage with an estimated 1.8 L blood loss over 4 minutes and uterus not contracting despite oxytocin and carboprost. She is a Jehovah's Witness who declined all blood products in a written advance directive countersigned during antenatal clinic, though has accepted cell salvage.

The consultant obstetrician and haematologist have been called in and are 10 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 78/44, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% on 15 L Hudson, temperature 36.3
data_table.Bloods (pre-op): haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 210 x10^9/L, fibrinogen 3.8 g/L, INR 1.1
data_table.Advance directive: declines packed cells, FFP, platelets, cryoprecipitate; accepts cell salvage, recombinant factor concentrates, tranexamic acid
data_table.Uterine tone: atonic despite oxytocin and 500 mcg carboprost given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Continue oxytocin and carboprost with warmed crystalloid resuscitation and await consultant arrival before further step
Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device and observe for 30 minutes while awaiting the consultant obstetrician arrival
Give O negative packed cells 2 units and fresh frozen plasma while continuing uterotonics as haemodynamic support
Activate cell salvage, give IV tranexamic acid 1 g, apply aortic compression, and prepare for hysterectomy urgently
Give recombinant factor VIIa 90 micrograms per kg IV as first-line pharmacological adjunct to achieve haemostasis now

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic timing after prelabour rupture of membranes at term in a colonised woman
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a healthy 32-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks and 1 day. Her waters broke clear four hours ago at home and she has just presented to the birth suite with mild irregular tightenings. Her routine 36 week vaginal-rectal swab returned Group B streptococcus positive. She has no reported drug allergies and has had a normal pregnancy.

Examination confirms speculum-visible clear liquor and a cephalic presentation at station -2 with a closed and posterior cervix.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Fetal: cardiotocograph normal, baseline 140, variability 10, accelerations present, no decelerations
data_table.Membrane status: ruptured at home 4 hours ago, clear liquor

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics until active labour is established and expectant management for up to 96 hours after rupture is complete
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g stat then 1.8 g every 4 hours until birth and plan for induction of labour if not established within 24 hours of rupture
Commence oral amoxicillin 500 mg eight-hourly and reassess in the morning if labour has not established with membrane-rupture rounding to 12 hours
Perform an emergency category-2 caesarean section to avoid vaginal GBS exposure to the neonate in this colonised woman in the current clinical setting
Give a single stat dose of IV cefazolin 2 g and manage as expectant until spontaneous labour without further antibiotic doses

subtopic_detail: Applying RANZCOG criteria for medical management with methotrexate
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the early pregnancy assessment clinic reviewing a 28-year-old para 1 with a positive urine pregnancy test and mild left iliac fossa discomfort for two days. Her last menstrual period was seven weeks ago. She has never had abdominal surgery. Her preferences discussed include a strong wish to avoid surgery if a safe alternative is available.

She is haemodynamically stable and reliable for daily blood tests and outpatient monitoring within a metropolitan area.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Abdomen: mild tenderness left iliac fossa, soft, no peritonism
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus with thickened endometrium; 2.2 cm mass in left adnexa without fetal cardiac activity; free fluid nil to trace in pouch of Douglas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG monitoring only, no intervention unless symptoms worsen or bhCG rises
Arrange urgent laparoscopic salpingectomy on the next available emergency list given the presence of an adnexal mass on ultrasound
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with day 4 and day 7 bhCG monitoring and clear return-if-worse advice
Two-dose methotrexate regimen (50 mg/m2 on day 0 and day 4) as the standard Australian protocol in the current clinical setting
Direct methotrexate injection into the adnexal mass under transvaginal ultrasound guidance in theatre today

subtopic_detail: Simultaneous BP control and eclampsia prophylaxis at term
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 34-year-old primigravida at 37 weeks and 3 days referred from her GP with a severe frontal headache and blurring of vision. She has no known chronic hypertension. On triage her BP is elevated and repeat readings 10 minutes apart confirm the finding.

She describes epigastric discomfort and reports reduced fetal movements today.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 96, blood pressure 178/116 (repeat 172/114), respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Reflexes: brisk with 3 beats of ankle clonus bilaterally
data_table.CTG: baseline 145, reduced variability 3-5 beats, no decelerations, no accelerations over 20 min
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): platelets 118 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 88 U/L (<40), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), urate 0.42 mmol/L, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral methyldopa 250 mg three times daily and admit for 24 hour observation with delivery deferred pending response to oral therapy in the current clinical setting
IV labetalol 20 mg with a 4 g IV magnesium sulfate loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour infusion, and prepare for expedited birth after obstetric consultant review
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg and reassess in 15 minutes before starting magnesium sulfate given the risk of neuromuscular blockade combination
Administer IV furosemide 40 mg to offload volume and reduce blood pressure via preload reduction before more targeted antihypertensive therapy
Empirical diazepam 10 mg IV over 5 minutes as eclampsia prophylaxis followed by BP monitoring every 15 minutes without antihypertensive therapy

subtopic_detail: Recognition and delivery decision at late-preterm gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 29-year-old para 2 at 34 weeks and 5 days referred by her midwife with two days of malaise and right upper quadrant pain. Her BP has crept up over the last week from 130/80 to 148/98 today. She had no problems in prior pregnancies. She has had no bleeding.

She describes a heavy sensation in the epigastrium and one episode of vomiting overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 100, blood pressure 148/98, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Abdomen: tender right upper quadrant, no guarding, uterus 34 cm SFH, cephalic, longitudinal, fetal heart 148
data_table.Bloods (RCPA): haemoglobin 96 g/L (110-140), platelets 62 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 285 U/L (<40), AST 340 U/L (<40), LDH 720 U/L (<250), bilirubin 32 micromol/L, film shows schistocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart with plan for birth after the second dose in an unhurried elective caesarean or induction
Transfuse two units of platelets prophylactically to bring the count above 100 and defer delivery decisions for 48 hours
Expectant management with weekly outpatient bloods and BP monitoring until 37 weeks aiming for spontaneous labour
Perform an emergency category-1 caesarean section within 30 minutes irrespective of fetal status or cervical favourability
Admit, commence IV magnesium sulfate, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM (first of two doses), plan birth within 24 to 48 hours by the safest route

subtopic_detail: Sequence of first-line manoeuvres when the anterior shoulder is impacted
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar attending a vaginal birth for a 35-year-old para 2 who is being managed by the midwife. The last pregnancy had a birth weight of 4.1 kg with a difficult delivery. Second stage has lasted 90 minutes and the head is now born but retracts against the perineum. Restitution has not occurred. The midwife has already made a call for help and started the buzzer.

The next contraction is expected in about 40 seconds and you have declared shoulder dystocia to the team.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.text: McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips onto the abdomen combined with a request to apply routine fundal pressure to expel the shoulder
Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement followed by emergency caesarean section as the first response to declared shoulder dystocia in the current clinical setting
Deliberate downwards traction on the fetal head with strong maternal pushing to attempt to disimpact the anterior shoulder immediately in the current clinical setting
Immediate deliberate fracture of the anterior clavicle to reduce shoulder diameter and permit delivery within the next contraction cycle in the current clinical setting
McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the maternal hips and suprapubic pressure directed downwards and laterally by an assistant while you attempt gentle axial traction with the next contraction

subtopic_detail: Combining latency antibiotics, corticosteroids and magnesium neuroprotection at extreme preterm gestation
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 26-year-old primigravida at 24 weeks and 3 days who presents with a gush of clear fluid and continued leaking. Speculum examination confirms pooling of amniotic fluid. She is afebrile and not contracting. She is very keen for everything possible to be done to give her baby a chance.

Her BMI is 22 and there is no history of urinary or genital infection during this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 88, blood pressure 116/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Speculum: pooling of clear amniotic fluid; cervix closed, long, no bleeding
data_table.CTG (variocam): baseline 145, variability appropriate for gestation, no contractions palpable
data_table.Ultrasound: single fetus 24+3, EFW 610 g, cephalic, AFI 4.2 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management bundle to commence in the next hour?

options.text: Immediate expedited birth by classical caesarean section at 24+3 given the extreme preterm gestation and risk of chorioamnionitis with expectant management in the current clinical setting

Latency amoxicillin with clavulanic acid 500/125 mg orally three times daily plus dexamethasone 12 mg IM stat and admission for observation only, without magnesium sulfate in the current clinical setting
Nifedipine 20 mg orally loading dose then 20 mg six-hourly for tocolysis and betamethasone alone; no antibiotics until symptomatic or biochemistry abnormal in the current clinical setting

Latency erythromycin 250 mg orally four times daily for 10 days, betamethasone 11.4 mg IM stat (first dose), and IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading then 1 g/hour for neuroprotection while awaiting neonatology counselling
Reassure and discharge home with weekly outpatient bloods and ultrasound; no admission or intervention required in the absence of infection or contractions in the current clinical setting

subtopic_detail: Surgical management decision when the contralateral tube is already absent
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar reviewing a 31-year-old para 1 presenting with acute right iliac fossa pain and lightheadedness. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago and a urine pregnancy test is positive. She had a right ruptured tubal ectopic three years ago managed by right salpingectomy. This morning she completed her family planning with her partner, who was hoping for a second child but is prepared to accept whatever is safest for her.

On ultrasound the current pregnancy is in her only remaining tube.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 106/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Abdomen: peritonism localised to left iliac fossa, mild rebound
data_table.Transvaginal ultrasound: empty uterus, 2.8 cm left adnexal mass with fetal cardiac activity present, moderate haemoperitoneum in pouch of Douglas
data_table.Prior surgical history: right salpingectomy 3 years ago for ruptured ectopic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative management?

options.text: Laparoscopic left salpingotomy to preserve the only remaining fallopian tube, accepting the associated 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast risk
Systemic methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM as the definitive treatment given the wish to preserve tubal function for future spontaneous pregnancy
Laparoscopic left salpingectomy with counselling that IVF is the recommended route to future pregnancy, given that the residual tube carries a high recurrence risk
Emergency laparotomy with left oophorectomy in addition to salpingectomy to remove any ovarian source of the pregnancy in the current clinical setting
Ultrasound-guided direct methotrexate injection into the ectopic sac followed by monitoring, avoiding surgical trauma to the last remaining tube

subtopic_detail: Choosing between uterine artery embolisation and peripartum hysterectomy after failed conservative surgery
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in theatre with the consultant obstetrician, anaesthetist and haematologist for a 36-year-old primipara who has bled 3.4 L after an uncomplicated vaginal birth. Uterotonics (oxytocin infusion, ergometrine 250 micrograms IM, carboprost 250 micrograms IM x3, and rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms) have failed. Bimanual compression and an intrauterine balloon achieved partial slowing. A uterine artery ligation with a B-Lynch brace suture has just been placed and bleeding continues at ~200 mL/5 min.

The interventional radiology suite is 15 minutes away and staffed within the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 82/48 on noradrenaline 8 microgram/min, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 98% on 15 L NRB, temperature 35.8
data_table.Coagulation: fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (1.5-4.0), INR 1.6, platelets 78 x10^9/L, thromboelastography reduced maximum amplitude
data_table.Transfusion: 4 red cells, 4 FFP, 1 cryoprecipitate given; MHP activated 20 minutes ago
data_table.Airway: intubated after fifth unit red cells for ongoing haemorrhage
data_table.Family: primigravida, expressed wish for future pregnancy antenatally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscular every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses in total while awaiting the interventional radiology team
Immediate intra-hospital transfer to interventional radiology for bilateral uterine artery embolisation as a fertility-preserving definitive intervention
Recombinant activated factor VII (NovoSeven) 90 micrograms/kg as the next haemostatic intervention prior to surgical escalation
Insert a second intrauterine balloon at higher inflation volume alongside the existing balloon to increase tamponade pressure
Proceed immediately to peripartum hysterectomy given failure of all conservative measures and ongoing life-threatening haemorrhage
